### 2. Collaborative filtering: "users like you"

Imagine a big grid. Rows are users, columns are products. A cell is 1 if the user bought or liked that product. This **user-item matrix** is enormous: crores by crores. It is also almost entirely empty. A typical user has touched maybe 50 out of 10 crore products.

**User-based CF** finds users like you and shows what they bought. It is intuitive, but slow at scale.

**Matrix factorisation** is the more practical idea. Instead of storing the giant grid, we learn two small tables:

- each user gets a vector of, say, 64 numbers: their **taste**;
- each item gets a vector of 64 numbers: its **character**;
- the predicted liking = the **dot product** of the two vectors. That means multiply matching numbers and add them up.

Training adjusts the numbers so predictions match known purchases. Nobody labels the 64 dimensions. But they often end up meaning things like "budget versus premium" or "fitness". Common algorithms are **ALS (alternating least squares)** for implicit feedback (clicks and purchases, not star ratings). Or a neural **two-tower model**, which does the same job with more features.

### 3. Content-based and embeddings

Collaborative filtering only knows *who bought what*. **Content-based** methods look at the product itself: category, brand, price band, title, description, image. If you viewed three cotton kurtas under 800 rupees, show other cotton kurtas under 800.

Modern systems turn titles and photos into **embeddings**, using text and image models. Nearby vectors mean "similar". To find the nearest few hundred out of crores in milliseconds, they use **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes, such as HNSW or FAISS. "Approximate" means very close to the true nearest, but much faster.

Note an important difference:

- "Also bought" usually wants **complements**: phone, then case.
- Content similarity gives **substitutes**: phone, then another phone.

Showing another phone right after someone bought one is a classic bad recommendation.

### 4. Cold start

- **New user**: no history. Show **popular items** in their city or category. Use context: device, location, the search that brought them in. Learn quickly from their first few clicks in this session.
- **New item**: nobody has bought it yet, so CF cannot place it. Use **content features**: its embedding sits near similar items. Give it some deliberate **exploration** traffic so it can earn data.

### 5. The two-stage system

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User opens app] --> B[Candidate generation]
    B --> C[Co-purchase, CF, trending]
    C --> F[Merge about 500 items]
    F --> G[Ranking model scores]
    G --> H[Business rules filter]
    H --> I[Top 10 shown]
    I --> J[Clicks logged for training]
```

**Stage 1, candidate generation**, is about **recall**: do not miss good items. It must be very fast and cheap. Several sources each return a few hundred items. These are merged and de-duplicated.

**Stage 2, ranking**, is about **precision**: put the best ones on top. A heavier model (gradient-boosted trees, or a deep neural network) scores every candidate. Its features include:

- **user features**: past categories, price range, brand liking, city, app vs web;
- **item features**: price, discount, rating, return rate, stock, delivery time to this pincode;
- **user-item features**: CF score, similarity to items in the cart, whether they viewed it before;
- **context**: time of day, sale day or not, the page they are on.

The model predicts probabilities like P(click) and P(buy). These are often combined as `score = P(click) * P(buy | click) * price weight`.

**Stage 3, rules and re-ranking**:

- Remove items already bought, unless they are consumable, like detergent.
- Remove out-of-stock items, and items not deliverable to the pincode.
- Apply **diversity**: no more than two from the same brand in a row.
- Respect sponsored or policy slots.

### 6. Offline precompute vs real time

- **Offline (batch, hourly or nightly)**: co-purchase tables, matrix factorisation, item embeddings, ANN indexes. Often also a precomputed "top 200 candidates per user". All written to a fast key-value store.
- **Near real time (seconds to minutes)**: a streaming job (for example Kafka plus Flink) updates "recently viewed", "in cart" and trending counts.
- **Online (at request time, within about 50-100 ms)**: fetch candidates, compute a few live features, run the ranker, apply rules.

Precompute is cheap but stale. Real time reacts to "she just searched for diapers", but costs more. Most systems mix both.

### 7. Evaluation

**Offline**, on held-out past data: hide each user's last purchases. Ask the system for its top k. Then measure:

- **precision@k**: of the k items shown, how many were actually bought or clicked. If 2 of the top 10 were bought, precision@10 = 0.2.
- **recall@k**: of the items the user actually bought, how many appeared in the top k.
- ranking metrics like **NDCG**, which reward putting the right item higher.

Offline numbers are only a filter. The real test is an **online A/B test**. Split users randomly. Show some the new model. Compare **CTR**, **conversion** and revenue per session. Watch guardrails like returns and latency. Clickbait can lift CTR without lifting sales.

### 8. Avoiding obvious and bad recommendations

- **Popularity bias**: popular items get shown, so they get clicked, so they look even better. Fix with normalisation, popularity penalties and some **exploration**.
- **Already bought**: do not show a fridge to someone who bought one yesterday. Do show refills for consumables.
- **Too similar**: ten nearly identical items waste the slots. Add **diversity**.

## A worked example

**Riya buys a phone on a Flipkart-like app during a festive sale.**

1. **Before purchase, on the phone's page.** The "also bought" widget fetches the precomputed co-purchase list for this phone's ID: back cover (score 0.71), tempered glass (0.64), 33W charger (0.40), earbuds (0.22). Rules drop the cheap cable that only scored well because it sells with everything. This is a single key lookup: a few milliseconds.
2. **She buys the phone.** The order event goes to a stream. Within a minute, the real-time layer marks "owns this phone model" and "bought a phone today".
3. **She opens the home page.** "Recommended for you" runs candidate generation:
   - co-purchase neighbours of her recent items: covers, glass and chargers for *that exact model*. About 150 items.
   - her matrix factorisation vector, nearest items by ANN. She previously bought fitness bands and running shoes. About 200 items.
   - trending in her city: about 100 items. Merged: about 400 candidates.
4. **Ranking.** The model scores each candidate. The back cover for her model scores high: high co-purchase, bought a phone today, cheap, fast delivery to her pincode. Another phone scores very low. The feature "bought a phone today" strongly predicts she will not buy another.
5. **Rules.** Remove her own phone and any phone in the same category for 30 days. Remove out-of-stock covers. Allow at most two covers in the top 10, so she also sees earbuds and a smartwatch strap.
6. **Display and logging.** The top 10 are shown. Every impression and click is logged with the model version, so tomorrow's training uses it.
7. **Measurement.** A new ranker adds "delivery time" as a feature. It is A/B tested on 5% of users for 2 weeks. CTR rises from 4.0% to 4.3%. Conversion rises from 0.9% to 1.0%. Returns are unchanged. It is rolled out.

## Common misconceptions

- **"It is one big AI that knows me."** It is usually a pipeline: several simple candidate sources, one ranking model, and many hand-written rules.
- **"Also bought means the products are similar."** Usually they are **complements** (phone and case), not lookalikes. Mixing these up gives "you bought a fridge, here are five more fridges".
- **"Higher offline accuracy means a better product."** Offline metrics use past data shaped by the old system. Only an A/B test on real users shows if conversion actually improves.
- **"Collaborative filtering understands the products."** It only sees who interacted with what. It cannot place a brand-new item. That needs content features.
- **"Recommend whatever sells most."** Popularity helps cold start. But personalisation must beat it, or it is not earning its cost.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Both widgets come from a recommendation system, with different inputs. 'Customers who bought this also bought' is item-to-item. From past orders we count how often two products are bought by the same people. We normalise so popular items don't dominate, and precompute a list per product. 'Recommended for you' is personalised. We use the user's history with collaborative filtering, typically matrix factorisation or a two-tower model. That gives every user and item an embedding. We add content-based similarity for new items. At scale it's a two-stage system. Candidate generation pulls a few hundred items quickly from several sources. Then a ranking model scores them using user, item and context features like price, rating, delivery time and recent activity. Business rules remove already-bought, out-of-stock and near-duplicate items, and add diversity. Heavy jobs run offline, and a streaming layer adds recent clicks. I'd evaluate offline with precision and recall at k. Then I'd decide with an A/B test on CTR and conversion, watching returns and latency as guardrails."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *How do you handle a brand-new product?* Use its content embedding (title, image, category) to place it near similar items. Give it a small amount of exploration traffic so it collects interactions.
- *Why two stages instead of one big model?* Scoring crores of items with a heavy model on every request is far too slow. Cheap retrieval narrows it to hundreds. The expensive model only scores those.
- *What would you watch during a big sale?* Stock and price freshness, latency at peak, and a fallback to precomputed popular lists if ranking is slow.

## Key takeaways

- **"Also bought"** is item-to-item co-purchase. **"Recommended for you"** is personalised from your history.
- Co-purchase counts must be **normalised**, so popular items do not appear everywhere.
- **Collaborative filtering** learns from similar users. **Matrix factorisation** compresses taste into small **embeddings**.
- **Content-based** features and embeddings solve **cold start** for new items.
- Real systems use **candidate generation, then ranking**, followed by **business rules** and diversity.
- Heavy work is **precomputed offline**. A **real-time** layer adds recent behaviour.
- Judge models with **precision@k** offline, but decide with **A/B tests** on CTR and conversion.
- Avoid **popularity bias**, already-bought items and near-duplicates.

## Check yourself

1. In the 5-customer table, which item would "also bought" show first on the Phone page, and why is a raw count not enough in real life?
   Answer: Case, bought with the phone by 3 customers. Raw counts favour items that sell with everything, like a cheap cable. So we normalise, for example with cosine similarity or lift.
2. A new phone cover launched today. Why can't collaborative filtering recommend it, and what can?
   Answer: CF needs interactions, and the cover has none. Content-based features such as category, compatible model, title and image embeddings can place it near similar items, plus some exploration traffic.
3. Why split the system into candidate generation and ranking?
   Answer: Generation must be cheap and high-recall across crores of items. Ranking uses a heavier, more accurate model, but can only afford to score a few hundred items within the latency budget.
4. A new model raises offline precision@10 and CTR, but conversion drops. What might be happening, and what do you do?
   Answer: It may be showing attractive but unsuitable items, such as clickbait discounts or items that cannot be delivered. Treat conversion and returns as the decision metric, inspect what changed, and do not ship on CTR alone.

question: When a seller uploads 10 product photos, how does the app store them and show fast, small versions on every phone? How do image upload pipelines work?
answer: ## The short answer Meena sells kurtas on a Flipkart-like marketplace. She uploads 10 photos of a new kurta. A well-built app does **not** push those photos through its own servers. It does not save them in its database either. Instead, five things happen. 1. **Permission slips.** The app asks the backend for **pre-signed upload URLs**. These are short-lived, one-time "permission slips". Each one lets the phone upload one file **straight to object storage**. Object storage is an S3-like store built for big files. 2. **Facts, not bytes.** The database keeps only a small row per photo. The row has an **ID**, the **storage key** (the file's name inside the store), a **status** and some metadata. The image bytes are not in it. 3. **Background workers.** When an upload finishes, a message goes onto a **queue**. **Background workers** pick it up. They **validate** the file, **strip hidden metadata** (like GPS location), and **check it for unsafe content**. Then they **resize** it into several sizes: thumbnail, listing card and zoom view. Each size is saved as **WebP or AVIF**. These modern formats are much smaller than JPEG at the same quality. 4. **CDN delivery.** Shoppers' phones load images from a **CDN** (content delivery network). A CDN is a set of servers in many cities that keep copies close to users. The image URLs are **versioned**, so they can be cached for a very long time. 5. **Right size per phone.** The page uses **responsive images** (`srcset`). A cheap phone on 4G downloads a 30 KB image, not a 4 MB original. Two extra pieces keep it healthy. **Lifecycle rules** move or delete old files to control storage cost. **Idempotent retries** let a failed step run again safely. ## The intuition Think of a **photo studio with a big back-room warehouse**. - **The front desk** is your API server. It is small and busy. You don't want customers carrying heavy boxes through it. So the desk hands each customer a **numbered token**. The token lets them drop their box **directly at the warehouse door** for the next 15 minutes. That token is the **pre-signed URL**. - **The register** is the database. It says "box 42 belongs to seller S9, received, not yet processed". The desk keeps the register, not the boxes. - **The conveyor belt** is the queue. Workers in the back take boxes off it. They check the box isn't empty or dangerous. They peel off private labels. They make **several prints in different sizes**: passport, postcard and poster. - **Neighbourhood kiosks** are the CDN. The prints go there, so customers pick them up nearby. A few words we will use: - **Object storage**: a service like Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or MinIO. It stores files ("objects") by a **key**, like `originals/9f2c`. It is cheap, almost unlimited and very durable. - **Pre-signed URL**: a web address with a **cryptographic signature** and an **expiry time** baked in. Anyone holding it can do exactly one allowed action, like "PUT this key", until it expires. - **Queue**: a list of jobs waiting to be done. Kafka, SQS and RabbitMQ are common ones. - **Variant**: one processed version of an image, like the 400-pixel-wide WebP. - **Idempotent**: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. ## How it actually works Start small: Meena uploads 3 photos and one shopper, Shreya, looks at them. The CDN keeps a copy, so the next shopper nearby is served straight from the edge.", "send": [{"from": "store", "to": "cdn", "label": "35 KB", "color": "a"}, {"from": "cdn", "to": "shop", "label": "35 KB", "color": "a"}], "highlight": ["shop"]}]} ``` ### 1. Keep image bytes out of the database You *can* put image bytes in a database column. That column type is called a BLOB, a "binary large object". It works for a small app. At scale it hurts. - **Size.** A phone photo is 3-6 MB. A million products with 8 photos each is roughly 30 TB. Database storage is expensive per GB. It is also slow to back up and copy. - **Wrong tool for serving.** Every image view would hit the database. Object storage plus a CDN is built for billions of file reads. So the rule is simple: **bytes in object storage, facts in the database**. ### 2. Give every file a clean key Object storage has no real folders. A key is just a string. A common layout: ``` originals/{imageId} -- private, never served directly variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w400.webp variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w800.avif ``` Use a **random ID** (like a UUID) instead of the seller's filename. Filenames clash, since every phone makes "IMG_0001.jpg". They can also leak private information. ### 3. Upload straight to storage with pre-signed URLs The phone asks the API: "I want to upload 10 photos." The API checks the seller and creates 10 rows with status PENDING. It returns 10 pre-signed PUT URLs, each valid for 15 minutes. The phone then sends the bytes directly to storage. Why this beats uploading through your API: - **Your API servers stay light.** They never hold 50 MB of photos per seller. They only sign URLs. - **Big files survive bad networks.** Storage supports **multipart upload**. It splits a big file into parts, so only a failed part is retried. That matters on patchy mobile networks. - **Limits go inside the signature.** You can fix the content type, the maximum size (via a signed POST policy), the exact key and a short expiry. In Java with the AWS SDK v2, signing looks roughly like this: ```java PresignedPutObjectRequest signed = presigner.presignPutObject(r -> r .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(15)) .putObjectRequest(put)); // put = bucket, key originals/{id}, image/jpeg return signed.url().toString(); // give this to the phone ``` The upload bucket stays **private**. Nobody can read originals from the internet. ### 4. Process in the background through a queue Storage reports "object created", or the app calls a confirm endpoint. Either way, a job goes on the queue. Workers do the heavy lifting **asynchronously**. That means the seller doesn't wait for it. ```mermaid flowchart TD U[Original uploaded] --> Q[Queue job] Q --> V[Validate file] V --> M[Strip metadata] M --> C[Moderation check] C --> R[Resize and encode] R --> D[Mark READY in DB] C --> X[Reject and notify] ``` Each step in plain terms: - **Validate.** Don't trust the file extension. Read the first bytes, the "magic number", to confirm it really is JPEG, PNG or HEIC. Enforce size and pixel limits, say 50 megapixels. This blocks **decompression bombs**: tiny files that expand into enormous images. Run the image library in an isolated container, because image parsers have had security bugs. - **Strip metadata.** Phone photos carry **EXIF** data: camera, time, and sometimes GPS location. Remove it. But first apply the **orientation** tag, or photos appear sideways. - **Moderate.** Automated checks look for nudity, violence, banned items, or text like phone numbers on the photo. Unclear cases go to a **human review queue**. - **Resize.** Make a fixed set of widths, keeping the shape: 150 (thumbnail), 400 (listing grid), 800 (product page) and 1600 (zoom). - **Encode.** **WebP** is typically 25-35% smaller than JPEG at similar quality. **AVIF** is often smaller still, but slower to encode. Keep a JPEG fallback for old devices. - **Write and publish.** Write the variants under a new **version** path. Then set the database row to `READY` with the version number. Only then does the product page use them. Rough numbers: one 4 MB photo becomes about 12 KB (thumbnail), 35 KB (400 px), 90 KB (800 px) and 250 KB (1600 px). That costs roughly 0.5-2 seconds of CPU. That is why it runs on workers that **scale with queue length**, not inside the request. ### 5. Deliver through a CDN with versioned URLs Shoppers never read from storage directly. The URL points at a CDN: ``` https://img.example-cdn.com/variants/9f2c/v3/w400.webp ``` **The version is in the URL.** So the file at that URL never changes. The CDN and the phone can cache it with: ``` Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable ``` That is one year. "Immutable" means the browser won't even ask whether it changed. When the seller replaces a photo, you write `v4` and point the product at the new URL. No CDN **purge** is needed. (A purge is a forced deletion of cached copies.) Old copies simply stop being requested. The CDN reads storage only on a **cache miss**. The bucket is locked, so only the CDN can read it. ```anim {"title": "Why the version lives in the URL", "w": 660, "h": 320, "intro": "The CDN keeps photos for a year. Meena then replaces photo 3. It ages out of the CDN. A lifecycle rule deletes v1 from storage 30 days later.", "highlight": ["st"], "remove": [{"node": "cdn", "index": 0}]}, {"say": "The trap we avoided: had v2 been written over the same URL, cached copies could show the old photo for up to a year.", "highlight": ["cdn"], "mark": [{"node": "cdn", "index": 1}]}]} ``` ### 6. Send each phone the right size A budget phone with a 360-pixel-wide screen does not need the 1600-pixel image. HTML lets the browser choose: ``` ``` - `srcset` lists the available files and their widths. - `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will be on screen. The browser then picks the smallest file that still looks sharp. It also accounts for screen pixel density. - `` with `` gives AVIF to browsers that support it. Others fall back to WebP or JPEG. - `loading="lazy"` delays images that are off-screen. Native apps do the same in code. They request the variant that matches the view size and screen density. ### 7. Control storage cost with lifecycle rules Storage is cheap per GB. But it grows forever if you let it. **Lifecycle rules** are policies on the bucket. They act automatically, by file age or key prefix: - **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 1 day. Half-finished uploads otherwise cost money silently. - **Delete abandoned uploads** still `PENDING` after 24 hours. - **Move originals** to a cheaper **storage class** (infrequent access or archive) after 30-90 days. They are kept only to regenerate variants. - **Delete old versions** of variants some days after they are replaced. CDN **egress** (data sent out to users) often costs more than storage. That is another reason small files pay off. ### 8. Make every step safe to retry Things fail. A worker crashes mid-resize. The queue delivers a message twice. A phone retries an upload on a flaky connection. So make every step safe to repeat: - **Fixed output keys.** The worker always writes `variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w400.webp`. Running twice just overwrites the same file with the same bytes. - **Conditional status update.** `UPDATE images SET status='READY' WHERE id=? AND version=? AND status='PROCESSING'`. A duplicate job changes nothing. - **Idempotency key on "create upload".** If the app retries the request, return the same image IDs. Don't create 20 rows. - **Retry with backoff, then a dead-letter queue.** Backoff means waiting longer between tries. A dead-letter queue is a parking area for jobs that keep failing, with an alert. One corrupt file then can't block the line. ## A worked example Now the real scale. **Meena lists her new kurta with 10 photos, during the run-up to a big festive sale.** 1. **She picks 10 photos.** They are 3-5 MB each, some HEIC from an iPhone. The app calls `POST /uploads` with the count, the file types and an idempotency key. 2. **The API checks and signs.** She is a verified seller, under her daily quota. The API creates 10 rows (`status=PENDING`, random IDs). It returns 10 pre-signed PUT URLs valid for 15 minutes. Each is locked to one key, `image/*`, and a 20 MB maximum. 3. **The phone uploads directly.** It sends 3 at a time to the storage bucket. Photo 7 fails halfway on a weak signal. The app retries only that file, with the same URL. The API never touches the 40 MB. 4. **Jobs pile up, workers grow.** Each completed upload puts a job on the queue. There is a sale-time backlog, so autoscaling has raised workers from 50 to 300. 5. **Photo 1 is processed.** The magic bytes say HEIC, and the size is fine. The worker rotates it per EXIF, then strips EXIF, which held GPS coordinates. Moderation says clean. It makes 150/400/800/1600 px versions in WebP and AVIF, plus a JPEG fallback. It writes them under `v1/` and sets the row to `READY`. About 2 seconds of work. 6. **Photo 9 is rejected.** Her phone number is printed on it. She sees "Photo 9 rejected: remove contact details". The other 9 go live. 7. **Shreya shops on a budget phone.** She lives in a small town and uses a cheap Android. The grid card requests `w400.webp` (35 KB) from the nearest CDN edge. On the product page, `srcset` picks the 800 px image. Pinch-to-zoom loads the 1600 px one, and only then. 8. **Meena replaces photo 3 next week.** The pipeline writes `v2/`. The product points at the new URLs. Phones see the new photo on the next page load, with no purge. A lifecycle rule deletes `v1/` 30 days later. ## Common misconceptions - **"Just upload to our API server and let it save the file."** That puts big, slow uploads on your most precious servers. It ties up threads and memory. Pre-signed URLs send bytes directly to storage. Your API keeps control through what it signs. - **"A pre-signed URL is a security hole."** It allows one action, on one key, for a few minutes. You still validate the file afterwards, because the client controls the bytes. - **"Purge the CDN whenever an image changes."** Purges are slow, rate-limited and easy to miss. **Versioned URLs** make changes instant and allow year-long caching. - **"Serve the biggest image and let CSS shrink it."** The phone still downloads all the bytes. That wastes data, battery and time. Use `srcset` and sized variants. - **"Storage is cheap, so keep everything."** Abandoned uploads, half-finished multipart parts and old versions add up to terabytes. Lifecycle rules clean them up automatically. Egress is often the bigger cost anyway. ## How to say it in an interview A 60-second script: *"I keep image bytes out of the database and out of my API servers. The app asks the API for pre-signed upload URLs. Each is short-lived, signed permission to put one file at one key in object storage. The phone uploads directly there. The database stores only a row per image, with its key, status and version. When the upload lands, an event goes onto a queue. Workers check the file by its real bytes, strip EXIF but keep orientation, and run moderation. Then they resize to a fixed set of widths and encode WebP and AVIF. They write variants under a versioned path, then mark the row ready. Shoppers fetch images through a CDN with versioned, immutable URLs. So we cache for a year and never purge. Replacing a photo just creates a new version. The page uses srcset, so each phone downloads only the size it needs. Lifecycle rules clean up abandoned uploads. Every step is idempotent, so queue retries are safe."* **Likely follow-ups:** - *Make all sizes upfront, or resize on the fly?* Making all sizes upfront ("eager") is predictable and cheap to serve. On-the-fly resizing behind the CDN suits new layouts. But the first request is slow, and you must whitelist sizes to stop abuse. Many systems mix both. - *How do you handle a sale-day spike in uploads?* The queue absorbs the burst. Workers autoscale on queue depth. The seller sees a "processing" status. Use separate queues so live listings go before bulk catalogue imports. - *Why not trust the file extension?* Anyone can rename a file. Check the magic bytes and pixel limits, and run the parser in an isolated container. ## Key takeaways - **Bytes in object storage, facts in the database.** Never store large images as database blobs at scale. - **Pre-signed URLs** let phones upload straight to storage. Your API only authorises. - Heavy work runs **asynchronously** on a **queue with workers**: validate, strip EXIF, moderate, resize, encode WebP/AVIF. - Serve through a **CDN** with **versioned, immutable URLs**. Change the URL instead of purging. - **Responsive images** (`srcset`, `sizes`, ``) mean each device downloads only what it needs. - **Lifecycle rules** delete abandoned uploads and old versions, and move originals to cheaper storage. - Make every step **idempotent**: fixed keys, conditional updates, retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue. ## Check yourself 1. Why give the phone a pre-signed URL instead of uploading through your API server? Answer: It sends large, slow uploads straight to object storage, which is built for them, so API servers don't hold the bytes in memory or tie up connections. The API still controls access by signing only one key, with a short expiry and type and size limits. 2. A seller replaces a product photo, but shoppers still see the old one for hours. What likely went wrong and how do you fix it? Answer: The new image was written to the same URL that the CDN and phones had cached with a long max-age. Write each change under a new versioned path and point the product at it, so caches fetch the new URL immediately and no purge is needed. 3. A queue delivers the same "process image" job twice. Why doesn't that create duplicate files or corrupt data? Answer: The worker writes variants to fixed keys that include the image ID and version, so the second run overwrites identical files. The final status update is conditional, so it changes nothing the second time. 4. Why strip EXIF metadata, and what must you do before stripping it? Answer: EXIF can contain private data like the GPS location of the seller's home, and it adds bytes. Before removing it, read the orientation tag and rotate the pixels, otherwise many photos will show up sideways.

question: A delivery agent marks orders as delivered while in a basement with no network. How does the app save that and sync it later without losing or mixing up data?
answer:
## The short answer

Ravi delivers parcels for a Flipkart-like app. He is in a basement with no signal. He taps **Mark delivered**. The app does not wait for the network to say "saved".

Instead, it writes the change into a **local database on the phone** first. At the same moment, it adds a small record to an **outbox**. The outbox is a queue of changes still waiting to go to the server. The screen updates right away.

When the network comes back, a **sync worker** sends outbox items to the server, oldest first. It **retries** on failure. Each item carries a unique **idempotency key**. So if the same request reaches the server twice, it is applied only once.

- **Nothing is lost**, because the change is on disk.
- **Nothing is applied twice**, because the key removes duplicates.

"Mixed up" data is handled in two ways:

- **Ordering.** Each change carries a per-device sequence number: 41, 42, 43. The server applies them in the order they happened. Phone clocks can be wrong, so clock time is only a hint.
- **Conflicts.** Maybe the same order changed on the server meanwhile. Say the customer cancelled. The server spots it with a **version number**. It settles it with a rule per field: **last-write-wins**, **server-wins**, **merge**, or **ask a human**.

The screen stays honest: "Saved on phone, 3 changes waiting to sync". Then a tick appears when the server confirms.

## The intuition

Think of a courier in an old building with no signal. He cannot call the office after each drop. So he writes each delivery in a **paper notebook**, with the time and a line number: "Line 7, order 4471, delivered, 2:14 pm".

When he walks out and gets signal, he reads out every unticked line to the office. He ticks each line after the office says "noted".

- **The call drops halfway.** He simply reads the unticked lines again. The office keeps a list of line numbers it has already noted. A repeated line is ignored. That list works like **idempotency keys**.
- **The office says "wait, the customer cancelled 4471 at 2:10 pm".** Someone must decide which fact wins. That is **conflict resolution**.
- **His watch is fast.** The line numbers still show the true order. That is why we prefer **sequence numbers** to clock time.

A few words we will use:

- **Offline-first**: the app is built to work fully without network. It uses the network when it can, but never needs it for a tap.
- **Local database**: storage on the phone, like SQLite, Room on Android, Core Data on iOS, or IndexedDB in a web app. It survives app restarts and phone reboots.
- **Outbox**: a table of pending changes, written together with the data change.
- **Idempotent**: doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.
- **Conflict**: two parties changed the same thing without seeing each other's change.
- **Version number**: a counter on a record that goes up by one on every change. It is used to detect conflicts.

## How it actually works

Start small: Ravi delivers 3 parcels in the basement. The animation follows them from tap to tick.

### 1. Write locally first, in one transaction

The key rule: **the data change and its outbox entry are saved together, in one local transaction**. A transaction means "all of it or none of it". Either both rows are on disk, or neither is. This is the same "transactional outbox" idea used on servers, just on the phone.

```java
db.runInTransaction(() -> {
    orderDao.updateStatus("OD4471", "DELIVERED", podPhotoPath);
    outboxDao.insert(new OutboxItem(
        UUID.randomUUID().toString(),   // idempotency key, made once
        nextSeq(),                      // per-device sequence: 41, 42, 43...
        "OD4471", "MARK_DELIVERED",
        baseVersion,                    // version the agent saw, e.g. 7
        System.currentTimeMillis(),     // device time: a hint only
        payloadJson));
});
```

If the app crashes one millisecond later, both rows are still there. Compare the bad design: write the order first, and keep the request only in memory. A crash would then lose the request forever.

### 2. The outbox and the sync worker

The outbox is a plain table. Its columns are `id`, `seq`, `entity_id`, `op`, `base_version`, `created_at`, `payload`, `status` and `attempts`.

A background worker runs when the phone's operating system reports network. On Android this is WorkManager; on iOS, BGTaskScheduler. It does four things:

1. Read pending items in `seq` order, in batches of, say, 20.
2. Send them to the server.
3. On success, mark them done (or delete them). Save the server's new version for each order.
4. On failure, leave them pending and retry later.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Agent taps Delivered] --> B[Local DB plus outbox]
    B --> C[UI shows pending]
    C --> D{Network up?}
    D -->|No| E[Wait and retry later]
    E --> D
    D -->|Yes| F[Send batch to server]
    F --> G{Server reply}
    G -->|OK| H[Mark synced]
    G -->|Conflict| I[Resolve by rule]
    I --> H
```

### 3. Retry with backoff and jitter

Retry with **exponential backoff plus jitter**. Backoff means each wait doubles: 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, up to a cap of a few minutes. Jitter adds a small random amount. Why? Picture 50,000 agents leaving a metro station at once. Without jitter, they would all hit the server in the same second.

Retry only **temporary** errors, like timeouts or HTTP 503. A **permanent** error, like HTTP 400 or a validation failure, goes to a "needs attention" state. It must not loop forever.

### 4. Idempotency keys stop double applies

Here is the classic trap. The phone sends "OD4471 delivered". The server saves it. The reply is lost as Ravi steps back into the lift. The phone thinks it failed, so it sends again. Without protection, the server might:

- record two deliveries,
- pay the agent twice, or
- send the customer two "delivered" SMSes.

The fix: the server stores each processed **idempotency key**. It uses a table with a unique constraint, kept for some days. If a key arrives again, the server returns the **saved earlier result** and does nothing new.

One detail matters a lot. The key is created **once, when the change is made**. It is not created on each retry. Otherwise every retry looks like a brand-new change.

### 5. Order by sequence numbers, not clocks

Phone clocks are unreliable. Users set them by hand. Dead batteries reset them. Time zones change mid-journey. A phone can easily be 10 minutes off, sometimes hours. So:

- **Order changes within one device by sequence number** (41, 42, 43). It never goes backwards, whatever the clock says.
- **Record two times.** Keep the device time: when the agent says it happened, useful for reports and disputes. Also keep the **server receive time**, which you can trust. The server can also estimate the clock error ("skew") at sync time.
- **Never let a wrong clock decide a conflict alone.** Say "latest timestamp wins" uses phone time. Then a phone set to next year wins every argument.

### 6. Version numbers reveal conflicts

Each order on the server has a `version`. The phone remembers the version it last saw, say 7. It sends that as `base_version`. The server checks:

- **Still version 7?** No one else changed it. Apply the change, set version 8, reply OK.
- **Now version 9?** Someone changed it meanwhile. That is a **conflict**.

This is called **optimistic concurrency**. There are no locks. The rule is just "apply only if nothing changed since I looked". When something did change, a rule decides the outcome.

| Strategy | How it works | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Last-write-wins (LWW)** | The latest change replaces the earlier one | Low-stakes fields: agent's notes, display preferences |
| **Server-wins** | The server value is kept; the phone's change is rejected | Money and authority fields: price, refund status, cancellation |
| **Merge** | Combine changes to different fields, or add both to a list | Independent fields: agent adds a photo, customer edits the landmark |
| **Ask the user** | Show both versions; a human decides | Rare, high-value cases; use sparingly in a delivery app |

Real systems mix these **per field**, not one rule for the whole record. A **domain rule** (a rule from the business itself) often beats a generic one. "Delivered" is a physical fact backed by a photo and GPS. So a later "cancel" from the customer cannot undo it. It should become a return request instead.

### 7. CRDTs, in brief

**CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)** are data structures built so any two copies can always merge automatically. The order of merging doesn't matter; the copies end up the same. One example is a counter where each device keeps its own count and the total is the sum. Another is the text structures behind collaborative editors, such as Automerge and Yjs.

They are excellent for **collaborative editing and offline notes**. For delivery status they are usually overkill. Business rules like "cancel after delivery becomes a return" are not something a generic merge can decide. Know what they are. Reach for them when many people edit the same data offline.

### 8. Show sync status honestly

An honest screen prevents panic and double work:

- **Per item**: a small clock icon for "saved on phone", a tick for "synced", a red mark for "needs attention".
- **A banner**: "Offline. 3 deliveries saved, will sync automatically."
- **Controls**: a "Sync now" button, and a clear message when something is rejected.
- **Guard the exits**: block logout or "clear app data" while items are pending, or warn loudly. That is one of the few ways to really lose data.

## A worked example

Now the real scale. **A Flipkart-like delivery app, festive sale week, a large apartment complex in Chennai.**

1. **Into the basement.** Ravi enters a basement parking area with no signal. He has 6 parcels for the tower. His phone clock is 9 minutes fast.
2. **First delivery.** For OD4471 he scans the parcel, takes a proof-of-delivery photo, and taps Delivered. The app writes, in one SQLite transaction: status `DELIVERED`, the photo path, and an outbox row. The row has key `k-91c2`, `seq = 41` and `base_version = 7`. The screen shows a clock icon. Total time: about 30 ms.
3. **Five more.** He delivers 4 more (seq 42 to 45). For OD4480 the customer refuses, so he marks it `RETURNED` (seq 46). The banner reads "Offline. 6 changes saved."
4. **Meanwhile on the server.** At 2:10 pm server time, customer support changed OD4480's delivery slot (version 4 to 5). The customer of OD4471 tried to cancel (version 7 to 8). That cancel was put on hold, because the parcel was already out for delivery.
5. **Back in signal.** Ravi comes up to the ground floor. Android reports the network. The sync worker sends seq 41 to 46 as one batch. The reply is lost when he steps into the lift. Backoff: retry after 2 s, then 4 s. The second retry succeeds.
6. **No duplicates.** The server sees key `k-91c2` and the others. Seq 42 to 45 were already applied by the first, "lost" attempt. So it returns the saved results: **no double delivery, no double payout**.
7. **Conflict on OD4471.** Base version 7, server version 8. The **domain rule** applies: delivery with a photo is a fact. Status becomes `DELIVERED` (version 9). The pending cancel becomes a return request. Ravi's phone is told the new version.
8. **Merge on OD4480.** Base version 4, server version 5. The changed fields differ (status versus slot). So the server **merges**: status `RETURNED`, slot unchanged.
9. **Clock skew.** All device times are about 9 minutes ahead of the server receive times. The server notes the skew and stores corrected times for reports. Nothing relied on them for ordering.
10. **Done.** Ravi's screen shows 6 ticks. Nothing lost, nothing duplicated, two conflicts settled by clear rules.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Just retry the HTTP call until it works."** If the app is killed or the phone reboots, an in-memory retry is gone. Pending changes must be **on disk**, in the outbox.
- **"Retries are safe by default."** Not for creating or changing things. Without an **idempotency key**, a lost reply plus a retry can apply the change twice.
- **"Use the phone's timestamp to decide who wins."** Phone clocks are often wrong. Use **sequence numbers** for order and **server versions** for conflicts. Keep device time as a hint.
- **"Last-write-wins is always fine."** It silently throws away the other change. For money, status and safety fields, use **server-wins or domain rules**.
- **"CRDTs solve all sync problems."** They guarantee that copies end up the same. They don't guarantee the result makes business sense. Most business workflows still need explicit rules.

## How to say it in an interview

A 60-second script:

*"I'd design it offline-first. When the agent taps Delivered, the app writes the status change and an outbox entry in one local SQLite transaction. So the change survives crashes and reboots, and the screen updates at once with a pending marker. A background sync worker sends outbox items in order when the network returns, with exponential backoff and jitter. Each change gets an idempotency key when it is created. The server stores processed keys, so a retry after a lost reply is not applied twice. For ordering I use a per-device sequence number, because phone clocks can be badly wrong. Device time is a hint; the server records its own receive time. For conflicts, each record has a version number. The phone sends the version its change was based on. If the server has moved on, a per-field rule decides: last-write-wins for low-risk fields, server-wins for money and cancellation, merge for independent fields. A domain rule says delivered with proof beats a later cancel. CRDTs suit collaborative data but are overkill here. Finally, the screen shows saved, synced and needs-attention states, and warns before logout with pending items."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *What if the outbox grows very large, say after a day offline?* Send in batches. Compress photos and upload them separately, with their own keys. Collapse repeated changes to the same order before sending, since only the latest status matters if nothing depends on the steps.
- *How long does the server keep idempotency keys?* Longer than the longest realistic offline period plus retries, for example 7 to 30 days. After that, version checks still block most stale replays.
- *How do you test this?* Airplane mode, killing the app mid-sync, dropping replies after the server commits, wrong clocks, and conflicting edits from two clients.

## Key takeaways

- **Write to the local database first.** The network is never in the path of a tap.
- Save the change and its **outbox entry in one local transaction**.
- A **sync worker** sends pending items in order, with **backoff and jitter**, and only retries temporary errors.
- **Idempotency keys**, created once per change, stop duplicates after lost replies.
- **Don't trust device clocks** for ordering. Use **per-device sequence numbers** and server time.
- **Version numbers** detect conflicts. Resolve them **per field**: LWW, server-wins, merge, or ask a human, plus domain rules.
- **CRDTs** merge automatically and suit collaborative editing, but don't replace business rules.
- Show **sync status** honestly: saved locally, synced, needs attention.

## Check yourself

1. The app updates the order row on the phone, then crashes before adding the outbox entry. What went wrong in the design, and how do you fix it?
   Answer: The two writes were separate, so the change exists locally but will never be sent. Write the data change and the outbox entry in one local transaction so both are saved or neither is.
2. The server applies "OD4471 delivered", but the reply is lost and the phone retries. Why must the idempotency key be made when the change is created, not when the request is sent?
   Answer: If a new key were made per attempt, the retry would look like a brand-new change and be applied again. A key fixed at creation time lets the server recognise the retry and return the earlier result.
3. A phone's clock is set two days ahead. Under "latest timestamp wins", what goes wrong, and what should be used instead?
   Answer: Every change from that phone would win every conflict, even when it is actually older. Use per-device sequence numbers for ordering and server version numbers to detect conflicts, keeping device time only as a hint.
4. The agent marks an order delivered offline; meanwhile the customer cancels it on the server. Which conflict strategy fits, and why not plain last-write-wins?
   Answer: A domain rule (or server-side rule) that a delivery with proof is a physical fact, so it stays delivered and the cancel becomes a return. Last-write-wins would decide on timing alone and could silently cancel a delivered parcel or drop the customer's request.

question: How can five people type in the same Google Doc at the same time without overwriting each other's words?
answer:
## The short answer

Picture a Flipkart-like marketplace team. Five people open the same sale plan in a Google Docs-like editor and all type at once. Nobody's words get overwritten. Why?

The editor **never sends the whole document around**. Each keystroke becomes a tiny **operation**, or "op". An op is a small change like "insert x at position 5" or "delete the character at position 12". Your screen applies your own op **instantly**. The op is also sent to the others.

The hard part: while your op travels, someone else may type earlier in the document. Then "position 5" points at the wrong place. Two main techniques fix this.

- **Operational Transformation (OT).** Before applying someone else's op, **adjust (transform) its position**. The adjustment accounts for edits made at the same time. A **central server** puts all ops in one agreed order. Google Docs is widely reported to use this approach.
- **CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types).** Give every character a **unique, permanent ID** instead of a number position. An op then says "insert after character ID such-and-such". Edits can be **merged in any order**, and everyone still ends up with the same text.

## The intuition

Imagine five friends writing one shopping list. Each has their own copy in a different room. They can only pass **sticky notes** through a messenger.

Sending a photo of the whole list would be a mistake. The last photo would **wipe out** everyone else's changes. So they send small notes: "add milk on line 3".

Now a problem. Sethu adds "eggs" on line 1. At the same moment, Arjun sends "add milk on line 3". When Arjun's note reaches Sethu, his list has shifted down by one line. "Line 3" now means a different spot. Sethu thinks: "I added a line above line 3 at the same time. So Arjun really meant line 4." That small correction is **transformation**.

The other approach: give every item on the list a **name tag** that never changes. Arjun's note says "add milk right after the tag called bread-7". However many lines move, everyone finds bread-7 and puts milk after it. That is the **CRDT** idea.

A few words we will use:

- **Operation (op)**: one small change, like insert or delete, with a position.
- **Concurrent edits**: two edits made at the same time, where neither person had seen the other's edit yet.
- **Converge**: everyone ends with exactly the same document.
- **Replica**: one copy of the document, on one person's device.
- **Latency**: the delay for a message to travel. It is often 50 to 300 ms on mobile networks.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why "send the whole document" fails

The simple design: every few seconds, upload the full text. The server keeps the latest copy. It breaks in three ways.

- **Lost updates.** Sethu and Arjun both download version 10. Sethu uploads his version. Then Arjun uploads his. Arjun's upload **overwrites** Sethu's words, because his copy never had them. This is the classic **last write wins** problem.
- **Locking does not help.** Lock the document while one person types, and four people wait.
- **It is wasteful.** A 200 KB document goes out on every keystroke, for a few bytes of change.

So we send **operations** instead. They are tiny, a few dozen bytes each. Then we design rules so they combine safely.

### 2. Send small ops, apply your own at once

Each change is a small message:

```
{ "type": "insert", "pos": 5, "text": "x", "user": "sethu", "baseRev": 41 }
{ "type": "delete", "pos": 12, "len": 1,  "user": "arjun", "baseRev": 41 }
```

`baseRev` means "I made this edit while looking at revision 41". A revision is one numbered version of the document.

The editor applies your op **on your screen immediately**. This is called **optimistic local apply**. So typing never feels slow. The op goes to the server in the background.

### 3. See the conflict in a tiny example

Two category leads, Asha and Ravi, edit a tiny document: `PAN`. Positions start at 0: P=0, A=1, N=2.

- Asha types `S` at the start: **insert S at 0**. Her screen shows `SPAN`.
- At the same moment, Ravi types `E` at the end: **insert E at 3**. His screen shows `PANE`.

Now each receives the other's op.

- Ravi applies Asha's "insert S at 0" to `PANE`. He gets `SPANE`. Correct.
- Asha applies Ravi's "insert E at 3" to `SPAN`. She gets `SPAEN`. **Wrong.** Her S shifted everything right by one.

The two screens now **disagree**. They will keep drifting apart. This is the core problem. Watch it, and the fix, step by step:

### 4. Fix it with Operational Transformation (OT)

OT uses a **transform function**. It takes two concurrent ops and adjusts one of them. The adjusted op still means the same thing after the other op has been applied.

For two inserts the rule is simple. If the other insert landed **before** my position, shift my position right by its length.

```java
// Rewrite op 'a' so it can be applied after concurrent op 'b'.
static Insert transform(Insert a, Insert b) {
    boolean bComesFirst = b.pos() < a.pos()
        || (b.pos() == a.pos() && b.userId().compareTo(a.userId()) < 0); // tie-break
    return bComesFirst ? new Insert(a.pos() + b.text().length(), a.text(), a.userId()) : a;
}
```

In our example, Ravi's "insert E at 3" is transformed against Asha's "insert S at 0". 0 is before 3, so it becomes **insert E at 4**. Asha's screen shows `SPANE`. Both screens match.

The **tie-break** matters. Say both people type at the same position. A fixed rule, here comparing user IDs, decides who goes first. Every replica makes the same choice. Real editors need similar rules for deletes and formatting. For example, a delete before you shifts you **left**.

**Why a central server?** Transforming ops correctly is famously hard when many people edit peer to peer, in any order. Several published OT algorithms were later shown to have bugs in tricky cases. The practical fix, used by Google Docs-like systems, is a **central server that decides one official order**:

1. The client sends its op with `baseRev = 41`.
2. The server has already accepted revisions 42 and 43 from others. It **transforms** the incoming op against 42 and 43. It stores it as **revision 44** and broadcasts it.
3. Each client transforms revision 44 against any of its own ops still waiting for an acknowledgement. Then it applies it.
4. A client usually keeps **only one batch of ops in flight** and buffers the rest. That keeps its logic simple.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Asha types S] --> B[Op sent to server]
    C[Ravi types E] --> B
    B --> D[Server picks one order]
    D --> E[Transform later op]
    E --> F[Save as next revision]
    F --> G[Broadcast to all editors]
    G --> H[Everyone shows SPANE]
```

### 5. The alternative: CRDTs

A **CRDT** avoids transforming positions at all. Instead of "insert at position 3", every character gets a **unique ID**. The ID is a pair `(counter, userId)`, like `7@ravi`. Every insert says "**put this after the character with ID X**".

- Asha inserts S after the special START marker.
- Ravi inserts E after the character `N`, whose ID is, say, `3@asha`.

Positions never appear in the op, so no shifting is needed. Two people may insert after the **same** character. Then a fixed tie-break on the IDs decides the order, the same on every device.

**Deletes** usually leave a **tombstone**. The character is marked deleted, but its ID stays. Why? Another person's insert might still say "after this character". Tombstones are cleaned up later, when it is safe. This clean-up is called garbage collection.

The big property: CRDT ops can be **applied in any order, even twice**, and every replica ends identical. So no central server is strictly needed. Open-source libraries such as **Yjs** and **Automerge** do this.

### 6. Compare OT and CRDTs

| | OT | CRDT |
|---|---|---|
| Position model | Numbers, shifted by transforms | Unique IDs per character |
| Needs central server | Practically yes | No, but often uses one anyway |
| Offline and peer to peer | Harder; long offline edits need many transforms | Natural fit |
| Memory | Plain text plus op log | Extra ID per character plus tombstones |
| Maturity | Decades of production use | Mature libraries now, newer at huge scale |
| Correctness risk | Transform functions are subtle | Merge is simpler to prove correct |

Neither is better in general. Mostly-online products with a strong server fit OT. Offline-heavy apps fit CRDTs.

### 7. Show cursors and presence

**Presence** means showing who is in the document and where their cursor is. These are the coloured flags with names.

- Cursor positions are small messages. They are **frequent but throwaway**, often limited to a few per second.
- They are **not saved** in the document history. If one is lost, the next one corrects it.
- A cursor is itself a position. So it is **transformed** (OT) or tied to a character ID (CRDT). Otherwise Ravi's cursor would jump when Asha types above it.
- They usually travel over a **WebSocket**, a long-lived two-way connection.

### 8. Handle offline edits

When the network drops, the editor keeps applying your ops locally and **queues** them. On reconnect:

- **OT:** the client sends its queued ops with the old `baseRev`. The server transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile. This works. But it gets expensive and full of edge cases after hours of separate editing.
- **CRDT:** the client just exchanges missing ops. Merging works in any order.

Either way, the merge is **automatic but not magic**. If two people rewrite the same sentence differently, both texts survive, mixed together. The system guarantees everyone sees the **same** result. It does not guarantee the result reads well. Humans fix the meaning.

### 9. Keep version history

The server's ordered **op log** lets it rebuild any revision by replaying ops. To keep that fast, it saves periodic **snapshots**: the full text every few hundred revisions. It replays only from the nearest snapshot. History groups nearby ops by author and time, instead of showing every keystroke.

## A worked example

Now the real scale. **The Flipkart-like marketplace team edits the festive sale launch plan.** Five people open the same document at 10 am, the day before the sale freeze. They are the programme manager, two category leads, a marketing writer and an engineering lead.

1. **Opening.** Each browser loads the latest snapshot plus recent ops, say revision 2,310. It opens a WebSocket and starts sending presence. Everyone sees five coloured cursors.
2. **Typing.** The electronics lead adds "Phones: 40% off" in section 3. The op `insert at 1,204` is applied on her screen instantly and sent to the server.
3. **Concurrent edit.** At the same time, the programme manager inserts 30 characters at position 150. His op reaches the server first. It becomes revision 2,311.
4. **Transform.** The electronics lead's op arrives with `baseRev 2,310`. The server sees that revision 2,311 inserted 30 characters before position 1,204. So it transforms her op to **insert at 1,234**. It stores it as revision 2,312 and broadcasts it. All five screens match.
5. **Same spot.** Two people type at the end of one sentence. The tie-break puts one first on every screen. **No words are lost.**
6. **Offline.** The engineering lead is on a train with no network for 20 minutes. He keeps editing the rollback section. His ops queue locally. On reconnect, they are sent with the old base revision. They are transformed against roughly 400 newer revisions, and merged.
7. **Mistake and recovery.** At 4 pm someone accidentally deletes the whole pricing table. The programme manager opens **version history**. She finds the 3:55 pm version, rebuilt from a snapshot plus replayed ops, and restores it. The restore is itself a new set of ops.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The server just keeps the latest full copy."** That causes lost updates. Real-time editors exchange small operations and merge them.
- **"OT and CRDTs guarantee the text makes sense."** They guarantee **convergence**: everyone sees the same thing. They also keep each person's characters. If two people rewrite one sentence, the result can still be messy. People resolve the meaning.
- **"CRDTs are always better than OT."** CRDTs make offline and peer-to-peer easier. But they cost extra memory per character, plus tombstones. OT with a central server is proven at very large scale. It depends on the product.
- **"Your typing waits for the server."** No. Ops are applied locally first. The server only decides the final order, and the transform keeps everyone consistent.

## How to say it in an interview

A 60-second script:

*"Sending the whole document fails, because the last upload overwrites everyone else. So a collaborative editor sends small operations, like insert x at position 5. It applies your own op on your screen immediately. The problem is that positions shift. If someone inserts text earlier at the same time, your position 5 now points somewhere else. Operational Transformation fixes this by adjusting each op against concurrent ops. For example, an insert shifts right if another insert landed before it, with a fixed tie-break for the same spot. A central server puts all ops in one order and broadcasts them. Google Docs is widely reported to work this way. The alternative is a CRDT. Every character has a unique ID, and inserts say put this after character X. So ops merge in any order, which is great for offline and peer to peer, at the cost of extra metadata. On top of that you add presence over WebSockets, an offline queue, and an op log with snapshots for version history."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *What if two people type at exactly the same position?* A fixed tie-break, such as comparing user or site IDs, puts one first. Every replica applies the same rule, so they converge.
- *Why does OT usually need a central server?* Transforming ops correctly in every possible order between many peers is very hard to get right. A server that fixes one global order reduces it to transforming against a known list.
- *When would you choose a CRDT?* When offline editing or peer-to-peer sync matters a lot, such as a field app or a local-first notes app. And when you can afford extra memory per character.

## Key takeaways

- Sending the **whole document** leads to **lost updates**. Send **small operations** instead.
- Apply your own op **locally first**, so typing never waits for the network.
- Concurrent edits make **positions shift**. Without a fix, replicas **diverge**.
- **OT** transforms each op against concurrent ops, with a **central server** setting one order. Google Docs is widely reported to use OT.
- **CRDTs** use **unique character IDs** and "insert after X", so ops **merge in any order**. Good for offline; costs memory and tombstones.
- A **fixed tie-break** makes same-spot edits converge.
- **Presence** (cursors) is separate, throwaway data, but still needs position adjusting.
- An **op log plus snapshots** gives version history and safe restores.

## Check yourself

1. Two people download version 10 of a document, edit, and upload the full text. What goes wrong?
   Answer: The second upload overwrites the first, because the second person's copy never contained the first person's changes. This is a lost update, which is why editors send operations instead.
2. The text is `CAT`. Meena inserts `S` at position 3 while Kabir inserts `B` at position 0. Using OT, what does Meena's insert become after Kabir's, and what is the final text?
   Answer: Kabir's insert is at 0, before 3, so Meena's op becomes insert S at 4. Both screens show `BCATS`.
3. Why does a CRDT not need to transform positions?
   Answer: Its ops refer to unique character IDs, such as insert after character 3 by Asha, not to numeric positions. IDs never shift, so ops can be applied in any order and still give the same result.
4. Why are cursor positions not stored in version history, and what must still happen to them when others type?
   Answer: Cursors are short-lived presence data; losing one is harmless because the next update corrects it, so saving them would only bloat history. They must still be transformed or tied to character IDs so they do not jump when text is inserted before them.

question: How does Google Maps calculate arrival time? Does it show the same for all users? People travel at different speeds, so how does it actually calculate arrival time, and how does it adjust for real-time traffic conditions?
answer:
## The short answer

Shreya is in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. At 6:00 pm she must drive to Whitefield, about 17 km away. She asks Google Maps. How does it come up with "arrive 7:15 pm"?

Google Maps sees the roads as a **graph of road segments**. A segment is a short stretch of road between two junctions. The **ETA (estimated time of arrival)** is roughly the **sum of the predicted time to cross each segment**. It adds **delays at turns, junctions and traffic lights**.

The key trick: each segment's time is predicted **for the moment you will actually reach it**, not for right now. If you leave at 6 pm, the stretch you hit at 6:40 is estimated with 6:40 conditions. This is called **time-dependent routing**.

The predictions blend three kinds of input:

- **Historical speed profiles**: how fast traffic usually moves on that segment at that time of day and day of week.
- **Live traffic**: anonymised, combined location and speed signals from phones with location sharing on. Plus incident reports: crashes, closures, Waze-style user reports.
- **Road attributes**: speed limits, road type, number of lanes, turn restrictions.

A machine-learning model combines these to forecast traffic from a few minutes to an hour ahead. Google has publicly described one built with **DeepMind using graph neural networks**.

**Is it the same for everyone?** Largely yes. Two users get essentially the same estimate for the **same route, departure time and travel mode**. It predicts how long the **typical traveller in the current traffic** takes, not how fast *you* drive. It differs when:

- the **mode** differs: car, two-wheeler in India, walking, cycling or transit;
- the **route** or **departure time** differs;
- you are already moving. The ETA is **recomputed continuously from your actual position**, which quietly corrects for your own pace.

## The intuition

Ask a seasoned Bengaluru auto driver, "How long to Whitefield?" He doesn't know how fast *you* drive. He thinks: "6 pm Tuesday. Agara is slow by now. Marathahalli bridge will be terrible by the time we get there. And a friend says there's a breakdown near Bellandur." He adds up each stretch and answers. Ask again halfway, and he updates from where you are. Google Maps does the same at planet scale, with millions of phones as its "friends".

Try a tiny trip first. Two segments, each 3 km. The first is clear now, at 30 km/h: 6 minutes. You will reach the second in 6 minutes. By then a school lets out and it drops to 15 km/h: 12 minutes. ETA = 18 minutes. Using "now" speeds for both would say 12 minutes, and be wrong.

Why does your own speed matter so little? In congestion, **the traffic flow sets your speed**. Careful and aggressive drivers both crawl at 12 km/h on the Outer Ring Road at 6:30 pm. On empty highways speeds vary more, and the system corrects as you go.

A few words we will use:

- **Segment (edge)**: a short stretch of road between two junctions. Junctions are the **nodes** of the graph.
- **Traversal time**: how long it takes to drive across one segment.
- **Speed profile**: a table of usual speeds for a segment, per time slot (say every 15 minutes), per weekday.
- **Probe data**: anonymised location and speed samples from moving phones, used to measure live traffic.
- **Time-dependent routing**: route search where a segment's cost depends on when you enter it.
- **Supersegment**: a group of neighbouring segments that behave alike in traffic.
- **Graph neural network (GNN)**: a model that lets each road "see" traffic on nearby roads.
- **MAPE (mean absolute percentage error)**: the average of |predicted minus actual| divided by actual. A common ETA accuracy measure.

## How it actually works

### 1. Model the roads as a graph

The map is a **directed graph**: nodes are junctions, edges are segments, and a two-way road is two edges. Each edge stores length, road type, speed limit, lanes and turn restrictions. Turns have a cost too. A right turn across oncoming traffic, or a U-turn at a median gap, costs more than going straight.

### 2. Follow the pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  P[Phone location pings] --> A[Anonymise per segment]
  I[Incident reports] --> F[Live traffic state]
  A --> F
  H[Historical speeds] --> M[Traffic model]
  F --> M
  M --> S[Time dependent route search]
  S --> E[Route and ETA]
  E --> S
```

The loop at the bottom: your new position keeps feeding route search.

### 3. Start from historical profiles

Past trips give each segment a usual speed per time slot and weekday, adjusted for holidays and events. This **baseline** knows Silk Board is slow at 6:30 pm before any live data arrives. It is the main guide for segments you will reach long after "now".

### 4. Add live traffic from phones

Phones with location sharing on send **anonymised** speed and position samples. Google has described combining them so individual trips cannot be identified, and dropping the start and end of each trip.

The samples are **map-matched** (snapped to the right segment), which is hard for stacked roads like a flyover above a service road. Then they are averaged per segment. The result is a **current speed** per segment, refreshed every minute or so. User reports, closures and incident feeds adjust it further.

Live data is noisy: one phone stopped at a tea stall looks like a jam. So it needs **enough samples** before trusting a reading, and filters out odd ones.

### 5. Predict: blend history with now

The core problem: **live data says what is happening now. You need what will happen when you arrive.** In 2020, Google and DeepMind publicly described a model that:

- groups neighbouring segments into **supersegments**;
- uses a **graph neural network**, so a jam spreading back from a junction informs each segment's forecast;
- predicts travel times from **a few minutes up to roughly an hour ahead**;
- cut the share of inaccurate ETAs a lot, by up to about half in some cities.

For a segment you will reach soon, the live reading dominates. For one you reach in 50 minutes, the forecast leans on history plus today's trend. A simplified picture, not Google's formula:

```
predicted_speed(seg, t_arrive) =
    w(horizon) * live_speed(seg)
  + (1 - w(horizon)) * hist_speed(seg, slot(t_arrive))
where w falls from about 1 at horizon 0 toward 0 as the horizon grows
```

The real model learns this balance from completed trips. It does not use a fixed weight.

**Quiet roads** are harder. Many residential lanes have few phone samples. There the model falls back on history, on the road's type and speed limit, and on similar or nearby roads. Accuracy is naturally lower there.

### 6. Search routes with time-dependent costs

Route search is a shortest-path problem (Dijkstra, A*, or faster precomputed variants such as contraction hierarchies). The twist: an edge's cost depends on **when you enter it**.

```
arrive = depart
for seg in route:
    arrive += travel_time(seg, arrive)      // predicted for when you enter seg
    arrive += turn_delay(seg, next_seg, arrive)
eta = arrive
```

That is why "leave now" and "leave in 30 minutes" can differ a lot. It is also why Maps can show a range like "typically 55 min to 1 hr 20 min" for a future departure.

### 7. Same for everyone? Mostly, by mode

| Factor | Changes the ETA? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Your personal driving speed | Barely, at planning time | The ETA predicts typical traffic flow. Your pace shows up only as you progress |
| Travel mode | Yes, a lot | Car, two-wheeler, walking, cycling and transit use different speed models and routes. Two-wheeler mode in India can use narrower roads and filters through traffic differently |
| Route | Yes | Different segments, different predictions |
| Departure time | Yes | Different time slots on each segment |
| Settings such as avoid tolls | Yes | Changes the route |
| Being mid-trip | Yes | ETA recalculated from your real position and time |

### 8. Re-estimate and reroute during the trip

Once you are driving, the app keeps recomputing the remaining route from your current location, with fresh live data. Drive faster than typical and the ETA drifts earlier; slower, and it drifts later. That is the **hidden personal correction**. If a much faster route appears, say because a crash blocks yours, the app offers or applies a **reroute**.

This explains **ETA jumps**. The ETA can sit still through a slow stretch it expected, drop sharply once you clear it, or jump up when a new incident is reported ahead.

### 9. Measure accuracy

Typical measures are **MAPE** against actual arrival, the **share of trips within a tolerance** (say 10 percent), and **bias** (always early or always late?).

In 2020 Google publicly said its ETAs were accurate for over 97 percent of trips. Rare events are the hardest: storms, sudden closures, cricket-match traffic.

## A worked example

**Shreya's commute: HSR Layout to Whitefield (ITPL), leaving 6:00 pm on a weekday, about 17 km.** The numbers are illustrative but realistic for that road. Speeds are predicted for the time you **enter** each segment.

| # | Segment | Length | Enter at | Predicted speed | Drive time | Junction delay | Reach end at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | HSR to Agara | 2.0 km | 18:00 | 18 km/h | 6.7 min | 1.5 min | 18:08 |
| 2 | Agara to Bellandur on ORR | 4.0 km | 18:08 | 15 km/h | 16.0 min | 1.0 min | 18:25 |
| 3 | Bellandur to Marathahalli bridge | 4.5 km | 18:25 | 12 km/h | 22.5 min | 2.0 min | 18:50 |
| 4 | Marathahalli to Kundalahalli | 4.0 km | 18:50 | 15 km/h | 16.0 min | 1.5 min | 19:07 |
| 5 | Kundalahalli to ITPL | 2.5 km | 19:07 | 20 km/h | 7.5 min | 0 | 19:15 |

**Planned ETA: about 75 minutes, arriving around 7:15 pm.** That is an average of about 13.6 km/h.

**Why time matters.** Suppose you used the speeds seen **at 6:00 pm** everywhere: say 18, 17, 16, 18 and 22 km/h. You would get about 58 minutes of driving plus 6 of junction delays. That is roughly **64 minutes**, about 11 minutes too short. The evening peak on the Marathahalli stretch builds between 6:30 and 7:00.

**Live update mid-trip.** At 6:20 pm Shreya is on segment 2. A truck breaks down on the Bellandur flyover. Within minutes, phones on segment 3 report about **8 km/h**. She will reach it in about 5 minutes, so the forecast trusts live data heavily. Say it blends to **8.8 km/h**. Segment 3 now takes 4.5 / 8.8 x 60, about **31 minutes instead of 22.5**. The ETA moves from 7:15 to about **7:23**. The app also checks other roads, such as Varthur Road. If one saves real time, it offers a reroute.

**Two users, same moment.** A colleague leaving by car at 6:00 pm sees the same 7:15. A two-wheeler rider sees a different, usually earlier ETA. A fast driver sees 7:15 at first, then drifts earlier.

**The e-commerce link: a Flipkart-like delivery promise and rider ETA.** The same ideas power last-mile delivery, with two key additions.

1. **Rider ETA for live tracking** ("your order arrives in 12 minutes"). It sums per-segment **two-wheeler** times along the rider's planned stops. Times come from past rider GPS traces by time slot, plus live speeds from the company's own riders or a maps provider.
2. **Doorstep dwell time.** This is time spent at each door: parking, gated-society security, lifts, OTP or cash on delivery. It is often bigger than the driving time. It is learned per area, building type and payment mode. Maybe 6 to 8 minutes for a Whitefield high-rise, 2 for an independent house.
3. **Careful quantiles for promises.** A quantile like P90 means "90 percent of cases finish within this time". The date shown at checkout is a **promise**. Breaking it costs trust and support calls. So it is set from a high quantile, say **P90 to P95**, of the total time across warehouse work, line haul and last mile. The live tracking ETA on the day uses the **median (P50)**. It is re-estimated continuously, and users want precision. During a festive sale, hub backlogs, not roads, cause most of the delay.
