question: A model scores 99% in testing but fails in the real world. What are overfitting and underfitting, and how do train, validation and test sets prevent it?
answer:
## The short answer

A Flipkart-like team builds a model to guess which orders will be returned. In testing it scores **99%**. After launch it flops. What happened?

Almost always, one of two things. The model **learned the test instead of the task**. Or **the test did not look like the real world**.

- **Overfitting** means the model memorised its training examples, including their noise and accidents. It did not learn the general pattern. It looks brilliant on data it has seen and weak on new data.
- **Underfitting** means the model is too simple, or too lightly trained, to capture even the real pattern. It is weak everywhere, on old and new data alike.
- **Train, validation and test sets** are three separate slices of data with separate jobs. The model **learns** from the training set. You **make choices** (which model, which settings, when to stop) using the validation set. You **measure once, at the end**, on the test set, which nobody has touched.

The split only protects you if it is honest. The most common cause of a fake 99% is **data leakage**: test or future information sneaking into training. And no split protects you from **distribution shift**, the world changing after launch. So you also need monitoring.

## The intuition

Think of three students preparing for a board exam with ten years of past papers.

- **Student A (overfitting)** memorises every past answer word for word. If the exam repeats an old question, she scores 100%. If a question is reworded, she is lost. She learned the papers, not the subject.
- **Student B (underfitting)** skims one chapter and decides "the answer is usually C". He scores badly everywhere.
- **Student C (good fit)** practises, tests herself on papers she kept aside, and understands *why* answers are right. She handles new questions.

Now map this to machine learning:

- **Training set** = the past papers you study from.
- **Validation set** = mock tests you keep aside to check your study method and decide what to revise. You may look at them many times.
- **Test set** = the real exam. You see it once. If you peek at it while studying, your score means nothing.
- **Data leakage** = a friend slipped you the real exam the night before. Your 99% is real on paper, but useless as a measure of what you know.
- **Distribution shift** = the board changes the syllabus after you studied. Even honest preparation can fail.

A few more terms:

- **Generalisation**: how well a model does on new data it has never seen. This is the only thing that matters in production.
- **Training error** and **test error**: the mistake rate on seen data and on unseen data. The gap between them is your clearest overfitting signal.
- **Hyperparameters**: settings you choose, rather than the model learning them. Examples: tree depth, learning rate, number of training rounds.

## How it actually works

### 1. A picture in words: a curve through dots

Imagine twenty dots that roughly follow a gentle upward curve. Each is a little off, because of noise (random wobble).

- **Underfit**: you draw a flat straight line. It misses the upward trend. Training error is high. Test error is high.
- **Good fit**: a smooth curve passing near most dots. It accepts small errors, because they are just noise.
- **Overfit**: a wild zig-zag that passes *exactly* through all twenty dots. Training error is zero. But between dots the line swings wildly, so a new dot lands far from it. Test error is high.

The overfit line learned the noise as if it were signal. That is the core idea, whether the model is a small regression or a large neural network.

### 2. Bias and variance in plain words

- **Bias** is error from being too simple or too stubborn. The model has strong built-in assumptions, like "everything is a straight line", and cannot bend to the truth. High bias causes **underfitting**.
- **Variance** is error from being too sensitive to the exact training data. Train it on a slightly different sample and you get a very different model. High variance causes **overfitting**.

The **bias-variance trade-off**: making a model more flexible usually lowers bias and raises variance. The sweet spot is in between. Here is how to read the two errors:

| Training error | Validation error | Diagnosis | What to try |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | High | Underfitting (high bias) | Bigger model, better features, train longer |
| Low | Much higher | Overfitting (high variance) | More data, regularisation, simpler model, early stopping |
| Low | Low, close to training | Good fit | Check for leakage, then ship carefully |
| Low | Low, but production is bad | Leakage or shift | Audit the split, compare live data to training data |

### 3. The three sets and their jobs

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[All labelled data] --> B[Training set]
    A --> C[Validation set]
    A --> D[Test set]
    B --> E[Model learns, checked on validation]
    C --> E
    E --> F[Final model chosen]
    F --> G[One final test score]
    D --> G
```

- **Training set**, often around 70-80% of the data. The model adjusts its internal numbers (weights) to reduce error here.
- **Validation set**, often around 10-15%. You compare models and hyperparameters here. You look at it again and again, so your *choices* slowly fit it. That is why it cannot be your final score.
- **Test set**, often around 10-15%. Locked away and used once at the end. If you tune after seeing it, it becomes just another validation set.

These percentages are illustrative. With millions of rows, 1-2% each can be enough.

### 4. Data leakage: the usual cause of a fake 99%

**Data leakage** means the model got information during training that it will not have when it makes real predictions. Common forms:

1. **Future information in features.** A fraud model uses "chargebacks on this account". But chargebacks are filed weeks after the order. At decision time that number does not exist. The feature almost *is* the answer.
2. **Duplicates across splits.** The same listing, complaint or near-identical image sits in both training and test. The model simply recognises it. This is common with scraped or user-generated data.
3. **Random splits on time-based data.** Shuffle a year of orders and the model trains on December, then gets tested on November. It has seen the future. For forecasting, fraud or churn, use a **time-based split**: train on the past, validate on the next period, test on the one after.
4. **Same customer on both sides.** The model learns that person, not the pattern. Use a **group split**, so each customer sits in one set only.
5. **Preprocessing on all data first.** Scaling numbers or filling missing values using the whole dataset leaks test statistics. Fit preprocessing on training data only.

A good rule: **for every feature, ask "would I know this value at the exact moment the prediction is made in production?"** If not, it leaks.

### 5. Cross-validation

With limited data, one validation set can be lucky or unlucky. **K-fold cross-validation** fixes this. Split the training data into K parts, often 5. Train K times, each time holding out a different part. Average the scores.

```java
// Pseudocode-style Java: 5-fold cross-validation
double total = 0;
int k = 5;
List<List<Row>> folds = splitIntoFolds(trainingRows, k); // group or time aware if needed
for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
    List<Row> valid = folds.get(i);
    List<Row> train = allExcept(folds, i);
    Model m = Model.fit(train);          // preprocessing fitted inside, on train only
    total += m.score(valid);
}
double cvScore = total / k;              // the test set is never touched here
```

Variants: **stratified** folds keep the class balance, which is vital for rare fraud. **Group** folds keep each customer in one fold. **Time-series** folds always validate on a later period.

### 6. Fixes for overfitting and underfitting

- **More data**: the most reliable cure. Noise averages out. **Augmentation** (cropped images, rephrased text) helps too.
- **Simpler model**: fewer features, shallower trees, fewer layers. Less room to memorise.
- **Regularisation**: a penalty for complexity, added to the training goal. **L2** pushes weights to stay small. **L1** pushes many to exactly zero. **Dropout** in neural networks randomly switches off parts of the network during training, so it cannot rely on any single path.
- **Ensembles**: combine several models, so one model's quirks average out.
- **Early stopping**: watch validation error during training. Training error keeps falling, but at some point validation error starts rising. Stop there and keep that version. The animation shows this.
- **For underfitting**, do the opposite: a more flexible model, better features, less regularisation, longer training.

### 7. Distribution shift after launch

Even a clean, leak-free model can fail later, because the world changes. **Distribution shift** means live data no longer looks like training data.

- **Data drift**: the inputs change. A festive sale brings new kinds of shoppers, new devices, new cities.
- **Concept drift**: the relationship changes. Fraudsters learn your model's blind spots, so yesterday's "safe" pattern becomes risky.
- **Label or feedback delay**: you only learn true outcomes weeks later, so problems show up late.

Defences: monitor inputs and prediction rates against a baseline. Track real outcomes. Retrain on a schedule or when drift alerts fire. Roll out in **shadow mode** (the model predicts, nothing acts on it) or to a small **canary** slice of traffic first. For language-model systems, LLM evals do the same job with test sets and regression checks.

## A worked example

**A "will this order be returned?" model for a Flipkart-like marketplace.** The goal is to flag risky cash-on-delivery orders before dispatch. Numbers are illustrative.

1. **First attempt.** The team takes 12 months of orders, shuffles them, and splits 80/10/10. A gradient-boosted tree model scores **99% accuracy** on the test set. Everyone celebrates.
2. **Reality check one: the metric.** About 8% of orders are returned. So always saying "not returned" already scores 92%. Precision and recall on returns tell the real story.
3. **Reality check two: leakage.** An audit finds two future features. "delivery_attempts" is known only after dispatch. "support_tickets_last_30_days" counts tickets raised *after* the order, often about the return itself. Removing both drops the score sharply.
4. **Reality check three: the split.** Random shuffling put the same sale-week orders in both training and test. The team switches to a **time-based split**: train on months 1-9, validate on month 10, test on months 11-12. They also use a **group split** by customer, so no buyer appears on both sides.
5. **Honest number.** With clean features and an honest split, recall on returns is a modest 60%, at a precision the business accepts. Lower, but true.
6. **Tuning.** Training recall was far above validation recall, so the model was overfitting. They cut tree depth and add regularisation and early stopping. They pick settings with time-series cross-validation on the training months. The test months are touched once.
7. **Launch.** Two weeks in **shadow mode**, then live for 5% of orders.
8. **Shift.** During the festive sale, first-time buyers from new cities flood in. Drift alerts fire and recall drops. The planned fallback: rule-based checks for brand-new customers during sale week, and a retrain using last year's sale data.

## Common misconceptions

- **"High test accuracy means the model works."** Only if the test set is clean, untouched, and looks like production. Leakage, a skewed metric, or a reused test set can all make a weak model look excellent.
- **"Overfitting just means training too long."** That is one cause. Others: too many features, too flexible a model, too little data, or over-tuning to one validation set.
- **"The validation set and the test set are the same thing."** The validation set is for decisions and is looked at many times. The test set is for one final, honest measurement. Using one set for both makes the score too rosy.
- **"Random splitting is always fine."** Not for time-based data, grouped data (same customer, same product) or near-duplicates. The split must mirror how the model will meet data in production.
- **"Once it passes testing, we are done."** Production data drifts. Without monitoring, a good model quietly decays.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Overfitting is when a model memorises its training data, noise included. It looks great on data it has seen and poor on new data. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it is poor everywhere. In bias-variance terms, underfitting is high bias and overfitting is high variance. To catch this, I split the data three ways. The model learns on the training set. I compare models and tune settings on the validation set, or with cross-validation when data is small. And I measure once, at the end, on a test set nobody has touched. When a 99% collapses in production, my first suspect is data leakage. That means features that would not exist at prediction time, duplicates or the same customer across splits, or a random split on time-based data. Fixes for overfitting include more data, regularisation, early stopping and simpler models. After launch I monitor for distribution shift, because even an honest model decays when the world changes."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *How do you spot overfitting quickly?* Compare training and validation error. A big gap, very low training error and much higher validation error, means overfitting. Both high means underfitting.
- *How would you check for leakage?* For each feature, ask whether its value is known at prediction time. Look for suspiciously strong single features. Check for duplicates and shared customers across splits. Confirm preprocessing was fitted on training data only.
- *When is plain cross-validation wrong?* When data has time order or groups. Use time-series folds (always validate on a later period) or group folds. Otherwise cross-validation itself leaks.

## Key takeaways

- **Overfitting** = memorising: great on seen data, poor on new data. **Underfitting** = too simple: poor everywhere.
- **Bias** is error from being too rigid. **Variance** is error from being too sensitive to the training sample.
- **Training set** to learn, **validation set** to choose, **test set** to measure once. Never tune on the test set.
- The most common cause of a fake 99% is **data leakage**: future information, duplicates, shared customers, or a random split on time-based data.
- **Cross-validation** gives a steadier estimate on small data, but folds must respect time and groups.
- Fix overfitting with **more data, regularisation, early stopping, simpler models and ensembles**.
- Choose a **metric that fits the problem**. Accuracy misleads on rare events like fraud or returns.
- After launch, **monitor for distribution shift** and retrain. Testing is not the finish line.

## Check yourself

1. A model has 98% training accuracy and 71% validation accuracy. What is the likely problem? Name two fixes.
   Answer: Overfitting (high variance), because the gap between training and validation is large. Fixes include more data, regularisation, early stopping, or a simpler model.
2. A demand-forecasting model was checked with a random 80/20 split of two years of daily sales. It looked excellent but fails in production. What went wrong?
   Answer: Random splitting on time-based data let the model train on days after the ones it was tested on, so it effectively saw the future. A time-based split (train on the past, test on a later period) gives an honest score.
3. Why can you not use the validation set as your final reported score?
   Answer: You looked at it many times while choosing models and settings, so your choices are partly fitted to it and its score is too rosy. The untouched test set gives the honest final number.
4. A fraud model worked well for six months, then its catch rate fell, with no code change. What is the likely cause, and what would you do?
   Answer: Distribution shift, most likely concept drift as fraudsters changed tactics. Monitor inputs and outcomes against a baseline, retrain on recent labelled data, and keep fallback rules while the new model is checked.

question: A fraud model is 99% accurate but useless. Why? Precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC explained with one example.
answer:
## The short answer

A Flipkart-like marketplace gets 100,000 orders a day. About **1 in 100 is fraud**. A "model" that simply says **"not fraud" for every order is 99% accurate**. And it catches **zero** fraud.

**Accuracy** is the share of all predictions that are right. When one class is rare, the big, boring class dominates it. So accuracy tells you almost nothing.

What you actually want to know:

- **Precision**: of the orders I flagged as fraud, how many really were fraud? (How often is my alarm right?)
- **Recall**: of all the real fraud, how much did I catch? (How much fraud slips through?)
- **F1**: one number that balances precision and recall. It is their **harmonic mean**, a kind of average pulled towards the smaller number.
- **ROC-AUC and PR-AUC**: how well the model **ranks** risky orders above safe ones, across every possible cut-off.

The right metric comes from **business cost**. What does a missed fraud cost? What does a wrongly blocked good customer cost? For fraud and medical screening you usually push recall. For spam filters you usually protect precision.

## The intuition

Think of a **security guard at a mall entrance** checking bags. Out of 100 people, 1 is carrying something they should not.

- A lazy guard waves **everyone** through. He is "right" about 99 out of 100 people. 99% accurate. Completely useless.
- A paranoid guard stops **everyone**. He catches the bad one, but annoys 99 innocent shoppers.

Two questions describe a guard much better than "how often were you right?":

- **Precision**: when you stopped someone, how often was it justified? Paranoid guard: 1 in 100. Bad.
- **Recall**: of the bad people who came in, how many did you stop? Lazy guard: 0. Bad.

Terms used below:

- **Positive class**: the thing we are trying to find, here fraud. **Negative**: everything else, the genuine orders.
- **Class imbalance**: one class is much rarer than the other, like 1% fraud and 99% genuine.
- **Score**: most models do not output yes or no. They output a number between 0 and 1, like "0.83 risk".
- **Threshold**: the cut-off you choose. A score above it means "flag as fraud".
- **Confusion matrix**: a 2x2 table counting the four kinds of right and wrong answers.

## How it actually works

### 1. The 99% trap, with numbers

Take **100,000 orders** a day, **1,000 of them fraud** (1%).

**Model A, "always genuine"**, predicts genuine for all 100,000.

- Correct: 99,000. Accuracy = 99,000 / 100,000 = **99.0%**.
- Fraud caught: **0 out of 1,000**.

**Model B, a real model** (illustrative numbers), flags 2,000 orders. 800 of them are truly fraud.

- Correct: 800 fraud caught + 97,800 genuine left alone = 98,600. Accuracy = **98.6%**.

Model B has **lower accuracy** than the dumb model. Yet it stops 80% of the fraud. **On imbalanced data, accuracy rewards doing nothing.**

### 2. The confusion matrix

Every prediction falls into one of four boxes:

| | Predicted fraud | Predicted genuine |
|---|---|---|
| **Actually fraud** (1,000) | **TP = 800** (true positive: caught) | **FN = 200** (false negative: missed) |
| **Actually genuine** (99,000) | **FP = 1,200** (false positive: false alarm) | **TN = 97,800** (true negative: correctly ignored) |

How to read the names: true or false = was the model right? Positive or negative = what did it predict?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  O[100000 orders] --> M[Model scores each order]
  M --> T{Score above threshold}
  T -->|Yes| F[Flagged 2000]
  T -->|No| P[Passed 98000]
  F --> TP[TP 800 real fraud]
  F --> FP[FP 1200 good customers]
  P --> FN[FN 200 fraud missed]
  P --> TN[TN 97800 fine]
```

### 3. Precision and recall in plain words

- **Precision = TP / (TP + FP)** = 800 / 2,000 = **40%**. "When we raise the alarm, we are right 40% of the time."
- **Recall = TP / (TP + FN)** = 800 / 1,000 = **80%**. "We catch 80% of all fraud." Recall is also called **sensitivity** or the **true positive rate (TPR)**.

Each mistake has a **different cost**:

- A **false positive** (low precision) means a genuine customer's order is held or cancelled. Cost: reviewer time, a delayed delivery, maybe a lost customer.
- A **false negative** (low recall) means fraud goes through. Cost: lost goods, a **chargeback** (the bank reverses the payment), and fraudsters learning you are easy.

### 4. The threshold trade-off

The model gives each order a score. **You** choose the threshold. Lower it and you flag more orders: recall goes up, precision goes down. Raise it and the opposite happens. Same model, different behaviour.

First, watch it with just 8 orders.

Now the real scale. Illustrative numbers for our 100,000 orders:

| Threshold | Flagged | TP | FP | Precision | Recall | F1 | False positive rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | 500 | 400 | 100 | 80% | 40% | 0.53 | 0.1% |
| 0.7 | 1,000 | 600 | 400 | 60% | 60% | 0.60 | 0.4% |
| 0.5 | 2,000 | 800 | 1,200 | 40% | 80% | 0.53 | 1.2% |
| 0.3 | 4,500 | 900 | 3,600 | 20% | 90% | 0.33 | 3.6% |
| 0.1 | 10,670 | 970 | 9,700 | 9% | 97% | 0.17 | 9.8% |

**False positive rate (FPR)** = FP / all genuine orders = FP / 99,000. It is the share of good customers you wrongly flag. Keep it in mind for ROC below.

"0.5" is **just a default**. The right threshold depends on costs, review capacity and **calibration**: whether a 0.3 score really means about a 30% chance.

### 5. F1: one number for both

**F1 = 2 x P x R / (P + R)**, the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is dragged down by the smaller number. So you cannot game F1 by maxing one side. Precision 100% with recall 1% gives an F1 of about 0.02, not 0.5.

At threshold 0.5: F1 = 2 x 0.4 x 0.8 / 1.2 = **0.53**. In the table, F1 peaks at 0.7.

F1 has limits. It **treats a missed fraud and a false alarm as equally bad**. It also ignores true negatives entirely. If costs are unequal, use **F-beta**. **F2** weighs recall more (good for fraud and medical screening). **F0.5** weighs precision more (good for spam). Better still, compute the actual rupee cost, as in the worked example.

A small Java helper makes the formulas concrete:

```java
record Counts(long tp, long fp, long fn, long tn) {
    double precision() { return tp + fp == 0 ? Double.NaN : (double) tp / (tp + fp); }
    double recall()    { return tp + fn == 0 ? Double.NaN : (double) tp / (tp + fn); }
    double accuracy()  { return (double) (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn); }
    double f1() {
        double p = precision(), r = recall();
        return (p + r == 0) ? 0 : 2 * p * r / (p + r);
    }
}
// new Counts(800, 1200, 200, 97800): precision 0.40, recall 0.80, accuracy 0.986, f1 0.533
```

### 6. ROC-AUC: how well does the model rank?

Instead of picking one threshold, try **all** of them. Plot **TPR (recall) on the y-axis against FPR on the x-axis**. That curve is the **ROC curve** ("receiver operating characteristic", a name from radar engineering). **AUC** is the area under it, from 0 to 1.

The cleanest intuition: **ROC-AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen fraud order gets a higher score than a randomly chosen genuine order.**

- 0.5 = a coin toss. No ranking skill.
- 1.0 = every fraud scores above every genuine order.

The catch: FPR divides by **99,000 genuine orders**, a huge number. At threshold 0.1 we wrongly flag 9,700 good customers. Yet FPR is only 9.8%, so the curve still looks great. **ROC-AUC can look rosy on heavily imbalanced data**, while precision is miserable.

### 7. PR-AUC: the honest view for rare positives

The **precision-recall curve** plots precision against recall across thresholds. **PR-AUC**, often reported as **average precision**, is the area under it. Its baseline is **not 0.5**. A random model scores roughly the **positive rate**, here **0.01**. So a PR-AUC of 0.45 on 1% fraud is a big lift over random, even though the number "looks low".

Rule of thumb: use **ROC-AUC for "can it rank at all?"** and for comparing models on fairly balanced data. Use **PR-AUC when positives are rare** and you care that the flagged list is clean.

### 8. Choose metrics from business cost

| Use case | Worse mistake | Lean towards | Typical setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Payment or order fraud** | Missed fraud is costly, but blocking good customers loses sales | High recall, at a precision the review team can handle | Score bands: auto-approve, manual review, auto-block |
| **Email or SMS spam** | Hiding a real bank OTP or job offer | High precision | Only filter when very confident; easy "not spam" button |
| **Medical screening** | Missing a sick patient | Very high recall | Positives go to a second, more precise test |

Also watch **review capacity**. A threshold that flags more orders than the team can check is useless.

### 9. Regression metrics in one paragraph

Sometimes the model predicts a **number**, not a class, like a delivery ETA in minutes. Then you use error metrics. **MAE (mean absolute error)** is the average size of the miss. If ETAs are off by 2, 4 and 12 minutes, MAE = 6 minutes. It is easy to explain and treats every minute equally. **RMSE (root mean squared error)** squares the errors, averages them, then takes the square root: sqrt((4 + 16 + 144) / 3), about **7.4 minutes**. Squaring punishes **big misses** much more. Use RMSE when one 40-minute miss is far worse than four 10-minute misses, because customers forgive small slips, not huge ones.

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like marketplace scoring cash-on-delivery and card orders for fraud during a festive sale.**

1. **Baseline.** 100,000 orders a day, 1% fraud. The team reports "98.6% accurate". But doing nothing scores 99%. So accuracy is dropped from the dashboard.
2. **Agree costs with finance and customer experience teams** (illustrative). An average missed fraud loses **₹5,000** in goods plus chargeback. A false flag costs about **₹200** in reviewer time, delay and some lost goodwill.
3. **Cost per threshold** = FN x ₹5,000 + FP x ₹200, using the table above:

| Threshold | FN | FP | Fraud loss | False-alarm cost | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | 600 | 100 | ₹30.0 L | ₹0.2 L | **₹30.2 L** |
| 0.7 | 400 | 400 | ₹20.0 L | ₹0.8 L | **₹20.8 L** |
| 0.5 | 200 | 1,200 | ₹10.0 L | ₹2.4 L | **₹12.4 L** |
| 0.3 | 100 | 3,600 | ₹5.0 L | ₹7.2 L | **₹12.2 L** |
| 0.1 | 30 | 9,700 | ₹1.5 L | ₹19.4 L | **₹20.9 L** |

(L = lakh = ₹1,00,000.)

4. **Read the result.** The cheapest thresholds are 0.3 to 0.5, **not** 0.7 where F1 peaks. F1 assumed both mistakes cost the same. Here a miss costs 25 times a false alarm, so the business wants more recall.
5. **Check capacity.** Threshold 0.3 flags 4,500 orders, but the review team handles 3,000. So they use **bands**. A score above 0.7 is auto-cancelled or asked for prepaid payment. 0.3 to 0.7 goes to manual review or an OTP re-check. Below 0.3 passes.
6. **Track weekly.** Recall (from chargebacks, which arrive weeks late), review-queue precision, PR-AUC for comparing models, and the rupee cost.

## Common misconceptions

- **"99% accuracy means a great model."** Only if 99% is far above the "predict the majority" baseline. Always compare against that baseline first.
- **"High ROC-AUC means few false alarms."** ROC-AUC measures ranking. With 1% positives, a model can have 0.95 ROC-AUC and still have most of its flags be wrong. Look at precision or PR-AUC too.
- **"The threshold is 0.5."** 0.5 is a default, not a decision. The threshold is a **business choice** made from costs and capacity. It can differ per segment, such as new users versus loyal users.
- **"F1 is the best single metric."** F1 assumes misses and false alarms are equally bad, and ignores true negatives. Use F-beta or a direct cost function when costs differ.
- **"A low PR-AUC like 0.4 is bad."** It depends on the base rate. With 1% positives the random baseline is about 0.01, so 0.4 can be strong.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Accuracy breaks when classes are imbalanced. If 1 in 100 orders is fraud, a model that says 'genuine' for everything is 99% accurate and catches nothing. So I look at the confusion matrix: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives. Precision asks: when I flag an order, how often am I right? Recall asks: of all the fraud, how much did I catch? The model outputs a score, and the threshold trades one for the other. Lower it, and recall goes up while precision goes down. F1 combines them, but assumes both mistakes cost the same. To compare models I use ROC-AUC, the chance a random fraud scores above a random genuine order. I also use PR-AUC, which is more honest when positives are rare. Then I pick the threshold from business cost. A missed fraud might cost 5,000 rupees and a false alarm 200, and the review team has limited capacity. Fraud and medical screening lean to recall; spam leans to precision."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *Why not just use F1 everywhere?* It weighs misses and false alarms equally. When a miss costs 25 times more, a cost function or F2 picks a better threshold.
- *When would ROC-AUC mislead you?* With rare positives. The false positive rate stays small even when you flag thousands of good customers, so the curve looks great. PR-AUC exposes that.
- *How do you measure recall in production if you only see what you flagged?* Use delayed labels such as chargebacks and complaints. Add a small random sample of unflagged orders reviewed by humans, to estimate what was missed.

## Key takeaways

- On imbalanced data, **accuracy rewards doing nothing**. Always compare with the majority-class baseline.
- The **confusion matrix** (TP, FP, FN, TN) is the source of every other metric.
- **Precision** = how often a flag is right. **Recall** = how much of the real problem you catch.
- The **threshold** trades precision against recall. It is a business decision, not a model property.
- **F1** balances both but assumes equal costs. Use **F-beta or a rupee cost function** when costs differ.
- **ROC-AUC** measures ranking. **PR-AUC** is the honest view when positives are rare.
- Choose metrics from the **cost of each mistake** and team capacity. Fraud and medical lean recall; spam leans precision.
- For number predictions, **MAE** is the typical miss. **RMSE** punishes big misses more.

## Check yourself

1. A disease affects 2 in 1,000 people. A test says "healthy" for everyone. What are its accuracy and recall?
   Answer: Accuracy is 998/1000 = 99.8%. Recall is 0%, because it catches none of the 2 sick people. Accuracy hides the failure; recall exposes it.
2. A model flags 500 orders. 300 are real fraud, and there were 1,200 fraud orders in total. What are precision, recall and F1?
   Answer: Precision = 300/500 = 60%. Recall = 300/1200 = 25%. F1 = 2 x 0.6 x 0.25 / 0.85, about 0.35.
3. Your fraud model has ROC-AUC 0.96, but the review team says most flags are good customers. How can both be true?
   Answer: ROC-AUC measures ranking and uses the false positive rate, which divides by a huge number of genuine orders. Thousands of false alarms still look like a small rate. With 1% fraud, precision can be low, so check precision at your threshold and PR-AUC.
4. For an SMS spam filter that might hide bank OTPs, would you favour precision or recall, and why?
   Answer: Precision. Wrongly hiding a real OTP or bank message (a false positive) is worse than letting some spam through, so only filter when the model is very confident.

question: Why did transformers replace older models like RNNs and LSTMs? What changed with "Attention Is All You Need"?
answer:
## The short answer

Shreya writes a long support chat on a Flipkart-like app. At the start she says she bought a **blue** phone. 500 words later she asks, "Will the replacement be the same colour?" To answer, a model must link a word at the start to a word at the end.

Before 2017, most language models were **RNNs** (recurrent neural networks: models that read text in a loop, one word at a time) and their improved version, **LSTMs** (long short-term memory networks). They carried a small "memory" forward. That design had two big problems:

- **Memory fades.** Early words get weaker as they are passed along. So long-range links are hard to learn, like a word at position 5 that matters at position 80. LSTMs reduced this. They did not remove it.
- **It is slow to train.** Word 50 cannot be processed until word 49 is done. GPUs are built to do thousands of things **at the same time**. A strict one-after-another loop wastes most of the hardware.

The 2017 paper **"Attention Is All You Need"** (Vaswani and others, at Google) introduced the **transformer**. It removed the loop completely. Every word looks at **every other word directly**, in one step. This is called **attention**. That fixed both problems: no fading chain, and the whole sentence can be processed **in parallel** during training.

Parallel training let people train much **bigger models on much more data**. Results kept improving fairly predictably as data, compute and model size grew. These patterns are called **scaling laws**. That is why transformers won.

The price: attention compares every word with every other word. So its cost grows with the **square of the input length**. Newer designs try to reduce this.

## The intuition

Imagine reading Shreya's long WhatsApp message **through a keyhole**. You see one word at a time. You cannot look back. You keep a short mental summary and update it after every word. By the end of 200 words, the first line is blurry. That is an **RNN**.

Now imagine the same message printed on one page. When you reach "it", your eyes jump straight back to "the parcel" in line one. You can do this for every word. And many people could each check different words **at the same time**. That is **attention**.

A few terms we will use:

- **Neural network**: a big function made of numbers. These numbers are called **parameters** or **weights**. Training adjusts them so the outputs get better.
- **Token**: a piece of text the model reads, roughly a word or part of a word. (Tokens, embeddings and context windows have their own answer in this app: "LLM concepts".)
- **Hidden state**: the RNN's running memory. It is a fixed-size list of numbers passed from one step to the next.
- **Gradient**: the training signal. It is calculated backwards through the network (**backpropagation**). It tells each weight which way to move.
- **Parallel** vs **sequential**: many calculations at the same time (what GPUs are good at) vs strictly one after another.

## How it actually works

### 1. How an RNN reads a sentence

An RNN keeps one hidden state, `h`. For each token, it mixes the new token with the old state. That makes a new state.

```java
// RNN: each step needs the previous step's result
float[] h = new float[HIDDEN];          // starts as zeros
for (int t = 0; t < tokens.length; t++) {
    h = tanh(add(matmul(W, h), matmul(U, embed(tokens[t]))));
}
// h must now summarise the whole sentence in a fixed number of values
```

There are two problems here. First, the loop **cannot be split up**. Step `t` needs `h` from step `t-1`. Second, the whole sentence is squeezed into one fixed-size `h`. That is a bottleneck for a 500-word review.


### 2. Vanishing gradients, and the LSTM patch

To train an RNN, the error at the end is sent backwards through every step. At each step, the gradient is multiplied by a number that is often smaller than 1.

- Multiply 0.9 by itself 50 times: about 0.005.
- Multiply it 100 times: about 0.00003.

So the signal from a late word barely reaches the early words. This is the **vanishing gradient problem**. The model cannot learn that word 3 mattered for word 90. If the numbers are bigger than 1, the opposite happens: gradients **explode**. That one is usually handled by **clipping** (capping the size).

The **LSTM** (from 1997) added a separate **cell state**. Think of it as a conveyor belt. Small learned switches, called **gates**, decide what to forget, what to write and what to read. Information can ride the belt with little change. So gradients survive over longer distances. **GRUs** are a simpler version of the same idea.

LSTMs powered speech, translation and phone keyboards for years. But they were a **patch**, not a cure. Memory still faded over hundreds of tokens. And training was **still sequential**.

Around 2014-2015, researchers added **attention on top of RNNs** for translation. It let the model look back at all input words. The 2017 paper asked a bold question: if attention does the useful work, do we need the loop at all?

### 3. What the transformer changed

The transformer keeps attention and **removes the loop**. Here is **self-attention** in plain words. It happens for every token at once:

1. Each token makes three lists of numbers (**vectors**). A **query**: what am I looking for? A **key**: what do I contain? A **value**: what I will pass on if chosen.
2. Each token compares its query with **every** token's key. A high score means "relevant to me".
3. The scores become weights that add up to 1. This step is called **softmax**.
4. The token's new meaning is the weighted mix of everyone's values.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Input tokens] --> B[Embeddings plus position]
  B --> C[Queries keys values]
  C --> D[Score every pair]
  D --> E[Softmax weights]
  E --> F[Mix values]
  F --> G[Feed forward layer]
  G --> H[Repeat N layers then output]
```

Other parts of the paper that matter:

- **Multi-head attention**: several attention "heads" run side by side. One head may track grammar. Another may track which noun a pronoun refers to. What each head learns is not hand-designed, and it varies.
- **Positional encodings**: there is no loop, so the model has no built-in sense of word order. Position information is added to each token. Otherwise "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same.
- **Encoder and decoder**: the original model was an **encoder-decoder** for machine translation. Later models used just the encoder (BERT-style, good for understanding and search). Or just the decoder (GPT-style, good for generating text). Most chat LLMs today are **decoder-only**.

### 4. Why parallel training was the real win

| | RNN / LSTM | Transformer |
|---|---|---|
| Steps to process 1,000 tokens in training | 1,000, one after another | Effectively one big step of matrix maths per layer |
| Path from word 1 to word 1,000 | 999 hops, signal fades | 1 hop, direct |
| GPU usage | Mostly waiting | Large matrix multiplications, which GPUs love |
| Cost of attention per layer | Grows linearly with length | Grows with length squared |

During training, the full sentence is already known. So the model predicts every next token **at the same time**. A **causal mask** stops tokens peeking at the words after them. The paper reported top translation results with far less training time than earlier systems.

One subtle point. When a decoder-only transformer **generates** text, it still produces one token at a time. The parallelism is mainly a **training** advantage. And training is where most of the cost and scale lives.

### 5. Scaling laws, in plain words

Once training could use thousands of GPUs well, labs tried bigger models. Around 2020, researchers published **scaling laws**. Grow **parameters**, **training data** and **compute** together, and the model's error falls along a smooth, predictable curve.

Later work, often called the **"Chinchilla" result** (2022), added a twist. Many models had been too big for the data they saw. **Data and model size should grow together.**

In plain words: **for several years, "make it bigger and feed it more" kept working.** You could roughly predict the gain before spending the money. RNNs never got this ride. Mainly, they could not be trained efficiently at that scale. Whether the curves continue forever is debated. Data, cost and energy are real limits.

### 6. The cost: attention is quadratic

If a text has `n` tokens, attention scores every pair. That is about `n × n` scores per head per layer. "Quadratic" just means "grows with the square".

- 1,000 tokens: about 1 million pairs.
- 10,000 tokens: about 100 million pairs. That is 10× the length but **100×** the work.
- 100,000 tokens: about 10 billion pairs.

While generating, the model also stores keys and values for every past token. This store is the **KV cache**. So memory grows with context length too.

Tricks like **FlashAttention** make attention much faster and lighter on memory. But they compute the exact same result. So the **compute still grows quadratically**. This is why very long context windows cost more and are slower.

### 7. Newer ideas, without the hype

Several families try to keep the quality but cut the quadratic cost:

- **State-space models** (for example the Mamba line of work) use a carefully designed loop that can still be trained in parallel. Cost grows roughly linearly with length. Memory stays fixed during generation.
- **Linear attention** variants rewrite or approximate attention. They avoid building the full `n × n` table.
- **Hybrids** mix a few normal attention layers with many cheaper layers. They aim for most of the quality at lower cost.

These are active research areas with promising results, especially for long inputs. But as of now, the **standard transformer is still the default** for most frontier models. Pure alternatives have not clearly replaced it.

## A worked example

**A shopping assistant on a Flipkart-like app reads Shreya's long chat and answers a question.**

The input is a 600-token conversation. Early on, Shreya says, "I bought the **blue** 6 GB variant for my father." Many lines later, after talk about delivery and a replacement, she asks: "Will the replacement be the same colour?"

**The LSTM way (the 2016 approach):**

1. It reads tokens 1 to 600 in order, updating one hidden state each time.
2. "Blue" was at token 12. By token 600 it has passed through nearly 600 updates. It may be overwritten by "delivery", "OTP", "pincode" and the rest.
3. Training on millions of conversations is slow, because each one is processed step by step.

**The transformer way:**

1. All 600 tokens are embedded with their positions.
2. When processing "colour" in the last question, attention scores it against every earlier token. "Blue" at position 12 gets a high score, because its key matches what "colour" is looking for. It is **one direct hop**, not 588.
3. In training, all 600 next-token predictions are computed at once. The GPUs stay busy. The team can train on far more conversations in the same time.
4. The cost: 600 × 600 = 360,000 attention scores per head per layer. Fine here. But suppose the team stuffs Shreya's full order history, say 50,000 tokens, into every request. Attention work grows about **7,000 times**. Latency and cost jump. A good engineer would **retrieve only the relevant orders** instead. That is the RAG idea, covered in its own answer.

**The lesson:** the model links distant facts well inside its window. But the window is not free. What goes into context is a cost decision (see "context engineering").

## Common misconceptions

- **"Transformers understand language; RNNs did not."** Both learn patterns from data. Transformers won mainly because they **train efficiently at scale** and link distant tokens directly.
- **"Attention was invented in the transformer paper."** Attention was already used with RNNs for translation a few years earlier. The paper showed you could **drop the loop** and build the whole model from attention plus simple layers.
- **"Transformers generate the whole answer in parallel."** Training is parallel. **Generation is still one token at a time.** That is why chat replies stream in word by word, and why output length drives latency.
- **"LSTMs completely solved vanishing gradients."** They **reduced** it a lot with gates and a cell state. But very long-range links stayed hard, and training stayed sequential.
- **"State-space models have already replaced transformers."** They are promising, especially for long inputs, and appear in some hybrid models. But transformers remain the mainstream choice today. The honest answer is "an open question".

## How to say it in an interview

*"RNNs and LSTMs read text one token at a time and carry a fixed-size memory forward. That caused two problems. First, information fades over long distances, because gradients shrink as they pass back through many steps. LSTMs added gates to reduce that, but did not remove it. Second, training is sequential, so it can't use GPUs well. The 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' paper removed recurrence entirely. Self-attention lets every token look at every other token directly, and the whole sequence is processed in parallel during training. That made it practical to train much bigger models on much more data. Scaling laws showed quality kept improving predictably with data, compute and parameters. The trade-off is that attention cost grows with the square of the input length, so long contexts are expensive. State-space models, linear attention and hybrids try to fix that, but transformers are still the default. For engineers, the lesson is that context length is a real cost and latency lever."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *If generation is token by token, why is it fast?* The KV cache stores past keys and values, so each new token does little new work. Output length still drives latency.
- *What does quadratic cost mean for a product?* Doubling the prompt roughly quadruples attention work. So you retrieve and trim context instead of sending everything. And you watch tokens per request as a cost metric.
- *What did LSTMs add over plain RNNs?* A cell state, like a conveyor belt, with learned gates. Gradients survive longer, but training is still one step after another.

## Key takeaways

- RNNs and LSTMs read **one token at a time** with a **fixed-size, fading memory**.
- **Vanishing gradients** made long-range learning hard. **LSTMs were a patch**, not a cure.
- Sequential training **wasted GPUs**. This was the bigger practical problem.
- The transformer **removed the loop**. Self-attention gives every token a **direct path** to every other token, and training runs **in parallel**.
- Parallel training enabled **scale**. **Scaling laws** showed more data, compute and parameters kept helping, predictably.
- The price: attention is **quadratic in input length**. Long contexts cost more time and money.
- **State-space models, linear attention and hybrids** are promising but have not displaced the transformer as the default.
- For engineers: treat **context length as a budget**. Remember generation is still token by token.

## Check yourself

1. An RNN is processing a 2,000-token document. Why can't you speed up its training on one document by giving it more GPUs?
   Answer: Each step needs the previous step's hidden state, so the 2,000 steps must run in order. More GPUs can process more documents side by side, but not the steps within one document.
2. In simple numbers, why do gradients "vanish" in a long RNN?
   Answer: The gradient gets multiplied by a factor at each step going backwards. If that factor is often below 1, say 0.9, then after 100 steps it is about 0.00003, so early tokens get almost no learning signal.
3. Your team increases the prompt for a support bot from 4,000 to 16,000 tokens. Roughly how much does attention work change, and what would you do about it?
   Answer: Length grows 4×, so attention work grows about 16×. Retrieve only the relevant history, summarise older turns, and track tokens per request as a cost and latency metric.
4. What was actually new in "Attention Is All You Need", given that attention already existed?
   Answer: It dropped recurrence completely and built the model only from attention, positional encodings and simple feed-forward layers, which allowed fully parallel training and direct links between any two tokens.

question: How does reinforcement learning work, and how is it used to train LLMs?
answer:
## The short answer

Shreya opens a Flipkart-like app during a festive sale. Which banner should she see first? The app can only try one, see if she orders, and learn. That is **reinforcement learning (RL)**: learning by trial and error.

In RL, an **agent** (the learner) takes **actions** in an **environment** (the world around it). It gets a number called a **reward** that says how good the outcome was. Over time it adjusts its **policy** (its rule for choosing actions) to collect **more total reward**. There is no labelled "correct answer" for each step, as in supervised learning. There is only feedback, often late and noisy.

For **large language models (LLMs)**, RL comes **after** two earlier stages. First, **pre-training**: predict the next token on internet-scale text. Second, **supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**: imitate good example answers. RL is then used in three main ways:

- **RLHF (RL from human feedback)**: humans compare pairs of answers. A **reward model** learns to predict their choice. The LLM is then optimised against that reward model, classically with **PPO** (Proximal Policy Optimization). A **KL penalty** keeps it close to the original model.
- **DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)**: skips the separate reward model and RL loop. It trains directly on the preference pairs with a simple, classification-style loss.
- **RL from verifiable rewards (RLVR)**: for maths, code and other checkable tasks, a program computes the reward (unit tests pass, the final answer matches). This is how **reasoning models** learn long chains of thought. **GRPO** is a popular, cheaper PPO variant used here.

The big risk throughout is **reward hacking**: the model learns to maximise the reward number, not the thing you actually wanted.

## The intuition

Think of training a new **delivery rider** in an unfamiliar city. Nobody gives a perfect route for every order. The rider tries routes. At day's end they see how many deliveries were on time and how customers rated them. Over weeks they learn which roads are fast at 6 pm, which shortcuts pay off, and when to stick with the known route.

The terms, mapped to the rider:
- **Agent**: the learner and decision-maker (the rider).
- **Environment**: everything outside that responds to actions (city, traffic, customers).
- **State**: what the agent knows right now (location, time, pending orders).
- **Action**: a choice it can make (turn left, take the flyover).
- **Reward**: a number saying how good it went (+1 on time, -1 late).
- **Episode**: one full run from start to finish (one day's shift).
- **Policy**: the strategy. It maps a state to an action, or to probabilities over actions.
- **Return**: total reward from now to the end. Future rewards are multiplied by a **discount factor** gamma, between 0 and 1. So near-term rewards count more. This is the **discounted** return.
- **Value**: the expected return from a state if you follow your policy ("how good is this junction at 6 pm?").
- **Exploration vs exploitation**: try a new road that might be faster (**explore**), or take the known decent road (**exploit**).

## How it actually works

### 1. The MDP: the standard frame

Most RL problems are written as a **Markov Decision Process (MDP)**. It has states, actions, **transition probabilities** (if I do action a in state s, where might I land?), a **reward function**, and a discount factor. "**Markov**" means the current state holds everything needed to decide. Older history adds nothing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Agent with policy] --> B[Takes an action]
  B --> C[Environment responds]
  C --> D[Reward and next state]
  D --> E[Update policy]
  E --> A
```

The hard part is the **credit assignment problem**. Suppose a customer rates a delivery an hour later. Which of the 50 earlier actions deserve the credit?

### 2. Value-based methods: Q-learning

**Q-learning** learns a **Q-value**, Q(s, a). It is the expected return of doing action a in state s, then acting well. The policy is simple: pick the action with the highest Q. After each step, it nudges its estimate toward a better target:

```
Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha * ( r + gamma * max_a2 Q(s_next, a2) - Q(s, a) )
```

- `alpha` is the learning rate (how big each nudge is).
- `r + gamma * max Q(next)` is the **target**: the reward just received, plus the best value it now thinks is reachable.
- The bracket is the **temporal-difference (TD) error**: how surprised the agent was.
- **DQN** (DeepMind, 2015) replaced the Q table with a neural network to play Atari games.

Q-learning suits **small, discrete action sets**. It is awkward when the action is "write a 500-token paragraph". You cannot take a max over every possible paragraph.

### 3. Policy-gradient methods

**Policy-gradient** methods skip Q-values. They directly adjust the policy's weights so that **actions that led to high return become more likely**. Actions that led to low return become less likely. The core idea is called REINFORCE:

```
for each sampled action:
    advantage = return_obtained - baseline     # better or worse than usual?
    loss     += -log_prob(action) * advantage  # push probability up if advantage > 0
```

The **baseline** reduces noise. It is often a learned **value function**, called the **critic**. You reward actions for beating expectations, not for being in a lucky episode. A method with both a policy (the **actor**) and a critic is called **actor-critic**.

**PPO** (Schulman et al., 2017) adds a safety rail. It **clips** each update, so an action's probability can move only about 20 percent from the old policy in one step. Big jumps tend to collapse training. That is why it became the default for LLMs.

Policy gradients fit LLMs naturally, because an LLM *is* a policy. The state is the prompt plus tokens so far. The action is the next token. The LLM outputs probabilities over that next token.

### 4. Bandits: RL with one step

A **multi-armed bandit** is RL with no state changes. Each round you pick one of K options ("arms"), get a reward, and repeat. A **contextual bandit** adds context (user, device, time) to each decision. This is the most common use of RL in e-commerce: banner ranking, recommendation slots, coupons, price-point tests, push-notification timing.

| Strategy | How it explores | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Epsilon-greedy | Random arm with probability epsilon, say 5 percent | Simple; explores blindly |
| UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) | Picks the highest optimistic estimate: mean plus an uncertainty bonus | Explores arms it knows least |
| Thompson sampling | Samples a plausible reward per arm from its current belief (its **posterior**), picks the best sample | Strong in practice, easy to batch |
| LinUCB / neural bandits | Reward modelled from context features | Contextual; personalises |

Compare a classic **A/B test**. A bandit **shifts traffic toward the winner while still learning**. So it loses less revenue. The loss is called **regret**: the gap between what you earned and what the best arm would have earned. The cost: messier statistics. For decisions needing clean cause-and-effect measurement, a fixed A/B test is still better.

### 5. RLHF: aligning an LLM to human preferences

This pipeline was publicly described in OpenAI's InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) and Anthropic's helpful-and-harmless work (Bai et al., 2022):

1. **SFT**: fine-tune the pre-trained model on human-written examples. This gives a decent starting policy.
2. **Collect preferences**: for many prompts, sample two or more answers. Human raters say which is better.
3. **Train a reward model (RM)**: usually the same architecture with a single-number output. It is trained so the preferred answer scores higher. The loss is the Bradley-Terry loss: `-log sigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected)`.
4. **RL with PPO**: the LLM answers fresh prompts. The RM scores each finished answer. PPO updates the LLM. The reward is `RM_score - beta * KL(policy || SFT_model)`.

**KL** means Kullback-Leibler divergence. It measures how far one probability distribution has drifted from another. The **KL penalty** stops the model drifting into weird text that happens to fool the RM.

PPO-based RLHF needs four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model and critic. That is expensive and finicky.

### 6. DPO: preferences without the RL loop

**DPO** (Rafailov et al., 2023) showed mathematically that the KL-limited RLHF goal has a closed-form best answer. So you can train **directly on preference pairs**. The loss raises the chosen answer's log-probability relative to the rejected one. Both are measured relative to a frozen reference model:

```
loss = -log sigmoid( beta * [ (logp(chosen) - logp_ref(chosen))
                            - (logp(rejected) - logp_ref(rejected)) ] )
```

No reward model, no sampling, no critic. It is cheaper and more stable, and widely used for open models. The trade-off: it learns only from a fixed dataset (**offline**). PPO generates and scores **new** samples (**online**), so it can explore beyond the data. Which wins depends on the task and data. Many labs combine stages.

### 7. RL from verifiable rewards and GRPO

Some tasks have a checkable answer. Then you need no learned reward model: **a program is the judge**. Reward = 1 if unit tests pass or the final number matches, else 0. Sometimes a format reward is added. This reward is hard to fool, so RL can run far longer. Models learn to produce long reasoning, check their work and backtrack. This is the publicly described recipe behind reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek, 2025). OpenAI's o-series is described in similar terms at a high level.

**GRPO** (Group Relative Policy Optimization, from the DeepSeekMath paper, 2024) drops PPO's critic. For each prompt it samples a **group** of, say, 8 answers and scores them. Each answer's advantage is its reward **relative to the group average**, divided by the standard deviation. This saves a whole model's memory. It works well when rewards are mostly 0 or 1.

### 8. Reward hacking

**Reward hacking** (also called specification gaming) is scoring high in a way that breaks your intent. LLM examples:
- A reward model that likes long answers produces verbose answers.
- One that likes confident tone produces confident wrong answers.
- **Sycophancy** (agreeing with the user), because raters preferred agreement.
- A code model that special-cases the test inputs, or edits the tests.

This is **Goodhart's law**: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Defences: KL penalties, reward-model ensembles, hidden test sets, length normalisation and human review of samples.

## A worked example

**A contextual bandit for the home-page banner during a festive sale.**

The page has one hero slot and 12 candidate banners: Mobiles, Large Appliances, Fashion, a bank-offer banner and so on. The goal is **clicks that turn into orders**, not raw clicks.

1. **Frame it.** Each impression is one bandit round. **Context**: user segment, city tier, device, hour, recent category views, new user or not. **Arms**: the 12 banners. **Reward**: 1 if the user orders in that category within 30 minutes of clicking, else 0. Choosing "order" over "click" deliberately blocks clickbait banners, a form of reward hacking.
2. **Model.** One Bayesian logistic regression per arm (or a shared model with arm features) predicts P(order | context, banner). **Thompson sampling** draws a sample of weights per arm, scores, and serves the highest.

```python
def choose_banner(context, arms):
    scores = {}
    for arm in arms:
        w = arm.posterior.sample()           # plausible weights given data so far
        scores[arm.id] = sigmoid(w @ featurise(context, arm))
    chosen = max(scores, key=scores.get)
    log_impression(context, chosen, propensity=estimate_prob(chosen))
    return chosen
```

3. **Exploration in practice.** At 9 pm on day one, the new bank-offer banner has little data. Its belief is wide, so Thompson sampling shows it often enough to learn. By 11 pm it is clearly strong for tier-2 Android users and weak for iOS metro users. Traffic shifts automatically **per segment**. A single global A/B test would miss this.
4. **Delayed reward.** Orders arrive up to 30 minutes later. A **reward joiner** (a Kafka stream matching impressions to orders) updates beliefs every 5 minutes in mini-batches.
5. **Guardrails.** Floors guarantee each contractual (paid) banner minimum impressions. A cap stops one banner taking more than 70 percent of traffic. A kill switch reverts to a static ranking.
6. **Log the propensity**, the probability the policy gave the chosen arm. This enables **off-policy evaluation**: before launch, the team estimates a new policy's results on yesterday's logs using **inverse propensity scoring**. No live traffic is risked.
7. **Measure the outcome.** A 5 percent holdout keeps a uniform-random or static policy. The team can report extra orders with clean statistics.

Elsewhere, the support assistant might be tuned with **DPO** on pairs where agents preferred answers citing the correct return policy.

## Common misconceptions

- **"RL means robots and games, not business."** Contextual bandits are RL. They drive ranking, notifications and offers at most large marketplaces.
- **"RLHF teaches the model new knowledge."** Mostly it shapes **behaviour and style**: helpfulness, format, refusal boundaries. It uses knowledge learnt in pre-training. RLVR on reasoning is the stronger case for new ability, and how much it adds versus surfaces is still debated.
- **"The reward model is the ground truth."** It is a learned, imperfect stand-in for human judgement. Optimising too hard against it causes reward hacking. That is why the KL penalty exists.
- **"DPO is just better than PPO."** DPO is simpler and cheaper. Online RL can still win when fresh samples and exploration matter.
- **"A bandit replaces A/B testing."** A bandit minimises regret while learning. An A/B test gives clean causal estimates. Use bandits for continuous tuning, A/B tests for one-off decisions that need a defensible answer.
- **"More reward means a better model."** Only if the reward measures what you want. Track independent evaluations too.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Reinforcement learning is learning from consequences. An agent in some state picks an action, the environment returns a reward and a new state, and the agent updates its policy to maximise long-run discounted reward. The core tension is exploration versus exploitation. Value-based methods like Q-learning estimate how good each action is; policy-gradient methods like PPO directly make good actions more likely. In e-commerce the most practical form is the contextual bandit, for choices like which banner to show. Thompson sampling shifts traffic to winners per segment while still exploring, and we log propensities for off-policy evaluation. For LLMs, RL is post-training. RLHF trains a reward model on human preference pairs and optimises the model with PPO under a KL penalty. DPO gets a similar effect directly from the pairs. Reasoning models use verifiable rewards, like passing unit tests, often with GRPO. The main risk is reward hacking, so I'd pair the training reward with independent evals and guardrails."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *Why a KL penalty in RLHF?* To keep the policy close to the supervised model. It can't drift into odd outputs that exploit the reward model's blind spots, and it keeps fluency and knowledge.
- *Bandit or full RL for recommendations?* A bandit when each decision's reward is roughly independent (one slot, one click). Full RL when today's action changes tomorrow's state, like long-term engagement or inventory-aware pricing. That is much more complex and risky.
- *How would you evaluate a new ranking policy before launch?* Off-policy evaluation on logged data with propensities (inverse propensity scoring or doubly robust estimators). Then a small online ramp with a holdout.
- *What is GRPO's advantage over PPO?* It removes the critic by comparing each sample to its group's average reward. That cuts memory and complexity, and suits 0-or-1 rewards.

## Key takeaways

- RL = **agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy**. The goal is maximum **expected discounted return**.
- **Exploration vs exploitation** is the central trade-off. **Regret** measures its cost.
- **Q-learning** estimates action values. **Policy gradients / PPO** directly adjust action probabilities. LLMs are policies, so PPO-style methods fit.
- **Contextual bandits** are e-commerce RL's workhorse: banners, offers, notifications. Log propensities.
- **RLHF**: preferences, then a **reward model**, then **PPO with a KL penalty**. **DPO** trains straight on preference pairs.
- **RLVR** uses program-checked rewards (tests, exact answers) to train **reasoning models**. **GRPO** drops the critic.
- **Reward hacking** is the constant risk. Reward is a proxy, so watch independent metrics.

## Check yourself

1. Your banner bandit's reward is "click". After a week, a clickbait banner with a misleading discount dominates but orders are flat. What happened and how do you fix it?
   Answer: Reward hacking: the policy optimised the proxy (clicks), not the goal (orders). Change the reward to a conversion within a time window (or revenue or margin), add guardrails on creatives, and monitor orders independently.
2. Why does PPO-based RLHF include a KL penalty against the SFT model, and what would likely happen without it?
   Answer: The reward model is an imperfect proxy; without the penalty the policy drifts toward outputs that exploit its blind spots (verbosity, flattery, odd text), losing fluency and real quality. The KL term keeps it near the trusted starting model.
3. A team wants to train an LLM to write SQL for internal analytics. Would you use a learned reward model or a verifiable reward, and why?
   Answer: Mostly a verifiable reward: execute the SQL against a test database and check it runs and returns the expected result. It is cheap, hard to fool, and supports long RL runs (for example with GRPO); keep hidden test queries and checks for readability or cost to avoid hacking.
4. Why does the banner bandit log the propensity of each chosen banner?
   Answer: The propensity is the probability the policy gave that banner. It lets the team run off-policy evaluation, using inverse propensity scoring on logged data, to estimate how a new policy would perform before risking live traffic.

question: Where does training data for an AI model come from, and why is good labelled data harder to get than a good algorithm?
answer:
## The short answer

Shreya writes to a Flipkart-like app: "Money debited but order not placed." A model must tag this chat as **payment failed** and send it to the right team. To learn that, it needs thousands of past chats, each tagged with the right intent.

That is **training data**: the **examples a model learns from**. For most business models, each example is an **input plus the right answer**. A support ticket plus its intent. A product photo plus its category. A payment plus "fraud" or "not fraud". The right answer is called a **label**.

Training data comes from four main places:
- **Logs**: what users and systems already did (searches, clicks, orders, returns, agent actions).
- **User feedback**: thumbs up/down, "was this helpful?", a customer correcting the bot.
- **Human labelling**: trained people, in-house or from a vendor, tagging examples by written rules.
- **Public datasets**: open collections such as Wikipedia text, academic benchmarks or open image sets, subject to their licences.

The old rule still holds: **garbage in, garbage out**. A model can only be as good as its labels.

Good algorithms are now **cheap and shared**. Everyone has the same open-source libraries and pretrained models. Good labelled data is **slow, expensive and specific to you**. It needs clear definitions, trained people, quality checks, privacy care and constant refreshing as the business changes. That is why **data, not the algorithm, is usually the real moat and the real bottleneck**.

## The intuition

Think of teaching a new cashier to spot fake ₹500 notes.
- If half the notes you show as "fake" are real, they learn the wrong thing.
- If you only show old designs, they fail on new ones.
- If two supervisors disagree on what is "suspicious", the cashier is confused too.

**The teacher's examples matter more than the teaching method.**

Terms we will use:
- **Model**: a program whose behaviour is learned from examples, not written as rules.
- **Label**: the correct answer attached to an example ("intent = refund status").
- **Supervised learning**: learning from labelled examples.
- **Labelling guidelines**: the written rulebook labellers follow.
- **Inter-annotator agreement (IAA)**: how often two labellers give the same label to the same example.
- **Label noise**: labels that are wrong.
- **Active learning**: letting the model choose which examples humans label next.
- **Weak supervision**: making rough labels automatically from rules and signals, not by hand.
- **Synthetic data**: examples generated by a program, often an LLM, not collected from real life.
- **PII (personally identifiable information)**: data that identifies a person, such as a name, phone number, address or email.

## How it actually works

### 1. Where the raw data comes from

| Source | Example | Strength | Catch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logs | Search query, then click, then order | Huge, free, real | Clicks are not truth; biased by what you already showed |
| User feedback | Thumbs down on a bot answer | Directly about quality | Few people give it; angry users over-represented |
| Human labelling | Agents tag 5,000 tickets by intent | Precise, matches your definitions | Slow and costly; needs guidelines and checks |
| Public datasets | Open text or image collections | Quick start | Licences, different domain, may already be in a model's training set |

Logs give **implicit labels**. A click hints "relevant". A quick return hints "wrong product". Useful, but noisy: users misclick, or never scroll to the best result. A model trained only on logs learns to **repeat your current system's habits**. This is called **feedback-loop bias**.

### 2. Why labelling is the hard part

Writing training code takes days. A good labelled dataset for a new task often takes **weeks to months**. Why?
- **Defining labels is a product decision.** Is "Where is my refund?" a *refund* intent or an *order status* intent? Someone must decide and write it down.
- **Edge cases never end**: Hinglish, typos, two problems in one message.
- **Experts are scarce**: fraud or medical labels need specialists.
- **The world drifts**: new products and policies make old labels stale.
- **Errors are invisible**: a wrong label looks like a right one until the model fails.

### 3. Labelling guidelines and agreement

A **labelling guideline** is a short document. It has:
- the list of labels, with a one-line definition each;
- 3 to 5 clear examples per label;
- tricky cases with the correct answer;
- a rule for "none of these" or "unsure".

Then you measure **inter-annotator agreement**. Give the same 200 examples to two or three labellers. See how often they agree.

Raw agreement can mislead. If 80% of tickets are "order status", people agree a lot by pure chance. So teams use **Cohen's kappa**, a score that removes chance agreement. A rough guide:
- above about 0.8: strong;
- 0.6 to 0.8: usable;
- below 0.6: **the guideline is unclear, not that people are careless**.

Low agreement on one label tells you exactly which definition to fix. The real loop is: **draft guideline, pilot label, measure agreement, discuss disagreements, update guideline, repeat** until agreement settles.


### 4. Label noise

Even with good guidelines, some labels are wrong: fatigue, misclicks, rushed vendors. A few percent of random noise is often tolerable. **Systematic noise** is worse. If one labeller always marks "cancel order" as "refund", the model learns that mistake.

Ways to handle it:
- **Gold questions**: hidden examples with known answers, used to score labellers.
- **Multiple labels per item** for hard cases, then a majority vote.
- **Model-assisted review**: re-check examples where a trained model confidently disagrees with the label. Many turn out to be labelling mistakes.
- **Keep the test set extra clean**: double-label and review it. Otherwise every comparison is meaningless.

### 5. Active learning: label the confusing examples first

Say you have 1 lakh unlabelled tickets and budget to label 5,000. Which ones? Random picks waste money on easy, repetitive examples. **Active learning** loops like this:

```
labelled = small random seed set (say 500)
repeat:
    model = train(labelled)
    scores = model.predict_proba(unlabelled)
    pick = examples where top two class scores are closest   # model is unsure
    labelled += human_label(pick[:500])
until budget spent or accuracy stops improving
```

Labelling where the model is **least sure** spends human effort on the borders between classes. That is where a label teaches most. It often reaches the same accuracy with noticeably fewer labels. Mix in some random examples too, or the dataset stops looking like real traffic.

### 6. Weak supervision

Instead of labelling each example, experts write **labelling functions**. These are small rules that vote on a label, or stay silent.

```
if "refund" in text and "not received" in text: vote REFUND_STATUS
if order_status == "CANCELLED" in last 24h:    vote CANCEL_RELATED
if text matches "otp|login|password":         vote ACCOUNT_ACCESS
```

Each rule is noisy and partial. A combining step estimates how reliable each rule is. Open-source tools such as Snorkel do this. The result is **probabilistic labels** for thousands of examples, in hours. A model trained on them usually generalises beyond the rules.

Weak supervision is great for a **fast first version**. You still need a clean, hand-labelled test set to know if it works.

### 7. Synthetic data from LLMs, and its risks

An LLM can write 10,000 fake support tickets in an afternoon: "Write 20 angry Hinglish messages about a late refund." It can also act as a labeller for real tickets. This genuinely helps for **rare classes**, **new launches with no history**, and **testing edge cases**.

The risks:
- **It copies the generator's bias and blind spots.** Synthetic tickets tend to be cleaner, more polite and more uniform than real ones. A model trained mainly on them can test well and fail on real, messy text.
- **Wrong labels at scale.** An LLM labeller can be confidently wrong on your specific policy. Check a sample against human labels before trusting it (see the separate answer on LLM evals).
- **Model collapse.** Train models again and again on text from earlier models, and the rare, unusual parts of real data fade away. Research has shown outputs get blander and less diverse each generation. **Keep real human data as the anchor.** Track what share of the dataset is synthetic.

A sensible rule: synthetic data to **fill gaps and stress-test**. Real data to **train the core and to evaluate**. Never evaluate only on synthetic data.

### 8. Data versioning

Models change when data changes. So the dataset needs version control, just like code. Each training run should record **which dataset version, which guideline version and which labellers** produced it. Tools such as DVC or lakeFS help, or immutable dated snapshots with a manifest.

Without this, when accuracy drops, you cannot answer the first question: **"what changed?"** It also lets you delete one user's data and know exactly which models were trained on it.

### 9. Privacy, consent and PII

Support chats are full of names, phone numbers, addresses, and sometimes card or UPI details. Before data goes to labellers, vendors or an external LLM:
- **Have a lawful basis and purpose.** India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 expects data to be used for a stated purpose, with consent or another valid ground. Check with legal what your terms allow.
- **Mask PII**: replace phones, emails and addresses with tokens like `<PHONE>`. Spot-check the masking.
- **Minimise**: send only the fields the label needs.
- **Control access and retention**: labellers see only their batch. Delete raw exports after use.
- **Honour deletion requests**. This is where data versioning pays off.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw logs and tickets] --> B[Mask PII]
    B --> C[Pick examples]
    C --> D[Human or weak labels]
    D --> E[Quality checks]
    E --> F[Versioned dataset]
    F --> G[Train model]
    G --> H[Find unsure examples]
    H --> C
```

## A worked example

**Goal:** a Flipkart-like support team wants a model that tags each incoming chat, like Shreya's, by intent. Then it reaches the right queue or bot flow. The numbers are illustrative.

**Step 1: Define labels.** Product, support and operations agree on 12 intents: order status, delivery delay, cancel order, return request, refund status, payment failed, wrong item, damaged item, account access, offers and coupons, seller complaint, other. They write a 3-page guideline with examples. It includes rulings like: "Money debited but order not placed" is **payment failed**, not refund status.

**Step 2: Collect and clean.** They export 2 lakh recent chats, plus last year's festive sale week. They mask phones, emails, addresses and UPI IDs, and remove duplicates.

**Step 3: Pilot and measure agreement.** Three senior agents label the same 300 chats. Kappa is 0.62. Disagreements cluster on refund status versus return request. The guideline adds: "If the item has already been picked up, it is refund status." The next 300 reach 0.81.

**Step 4: Build a clean test set first.** 2,000 chats, sampled to match real traffic. Each is double-labelled, with a reviewer resolving conflicts. This set is frozen and never used for training.

**Step 5: Bootstrap cheaply.** Labelling functions use keywords plus order-system facts. For example, an order cancelled in the last day votes for cancel order. They create rough labels for 50,000 chats. A first model trained on them scores 78% on the clean test set.

**Step 6: Active learning.** Each week the model picks the 1,500 chats it is least sure about, plus 300 random ones. The vendor team labels them, with 5% gold questions to track quality. After four rounds (about 7,000 human labels), accuracy reaches 89%.

**Step 7: Fix a rare class.** Seller complaint has only 120 real examples. An LLM generates 800 varied examples. The team keeps only those two reviewers accept, and caps synthetic data at 15% of that class. Recall on seller complaint (the share of real ones caught) rises from 55% to 74%, measured on real test chats only.
