question: AI engineering: what are the 19 core concepts (from Neo Kim's list) and how do they fit together?
answer:
## The short answer

Neo Kim (@systemdesignone) published a list of **19 concepts** for getting good at AI engineering. Each one links to an article on his newsletter. As a flat list, it looks random. Grouped, it falls into **five layers**. Each layer builds on the one below.

| Layer | Concepts |
|---|---|
| **1. Model fundamentals** | (4) LLM concepts: tokens, embeddings, attention, context windows; (5) context engineering |
| **2. Knowledge and retrieval** | (2) RAG; (7) vector databases; (16) HNSW |
| **3. Agents** | (1) how AI agents work; (3) MCP; (8) designing an agent; (9) multi-agent architecture; (10) agentic patterns; (11) memory, state and consistency; (18) A2A protocol; (19) research agents; (15) a personal chat assistant |
| **4. Quality and adaptation** | (13) LLM evals; (12) fine-tuning; (14) reinforcement learning; (17) vertical small LLMs |
| **5. Production scale** | (6) scaling an AI app to 1M users |

The whole story in five short lines:

- A model predicts the next piece of text from what is in its **context window** (its working memory for one request).
- **Retrieval and tools** decide what goes into that window.
- An **agent** is a loop that keeps refilling the window.
- **Evals** (tests for AI output) tell you whether any of it works.
- **Fine-tuning, RL and small models** change the model itself when prompting is not enough.

Every concept has its own detailed answer in this app (see its own answer in Random thoughts). This answer is the map.

## The intuition

Start with Shreya. On a Flipkart-like app she types: "running shoes under 3000 for flat feet, delivered before Sunday". All five layers work on that answer.

Picture the assistant as a very well-read new hire. This hire has **no memory between conversations**.

- **Model fundamentals** is how the hire thinks. They read text in small chunks (**tokens**). They store meaning as coordinates (**embeddings**). They decide which earlier words matter for the next word (**attention**). They can hold only so much on their desk at once (the **context window**). **Context engineering** is deciding what goes on that desk.
- **Retrieval** is the filing cabinet. The hire does not memorise every policy. They look it up. **RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation) means "look it up, then answer". A **vector database** is the cabinet sorted by meaning. **HNSW** is the index that makes lookup fast.
- **Agents** are the hire being allowed to act: check an order, issue a refund, ask a colleague. **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is a standard plug for tools. **A2A** (Agent2Agent) is a standard way for agents to talk to other agents.
- **Quality and adaptation** is performance review and training. **Evals** measure the work. **Fine-tuning** and **reinforcement learning (RL)** retrain habits. **Vertical small LLMs** are hiring a specialist instead of a generalist.
- **Production scale** is running a call centre of these hires on sale day without going bankrupt.

## How it actually works

### Step 1: Model fundamentals

**(4) LLM concepts.** A large language model (**LLM**) is a neural network trained to predict the next **token**. A token is a word piece, roughly 3-4 English characters. Each token becomes an **embedding**: a list of numbers where similar meanings sit close together.

**Attention** is the core of the Transformer design (Vaswani et al., 2017). It lets each token weigh every earlier token when predicting the next one. Its cost grows with the length of the text. That is why the **context window** is finite. The window is the maximum tokens per request: from tens of thousands to around a million, depending on the model. Long prompts cost more and run slower. The output is **sampled** (picked with some randomness), so the same prompt can give different answers.

**(5) Context engineering.** The model only knows what is in the window right now. Context engineering is assembling that window. It holds system instructions, retrieved documents, tool definitions, chat history, memory and the output format. All of it must fit a **token budget**.

It has largely replaced "prompt engineering", because the hard part is choosing and ordering content, not wording. Too little context makes the model guess. Too much distracts it and costs money.

### Step 2: Knowledge and retrieval

**(2) RAG.** RAG fetches relevant passages when the question arrives. It adds them to the prompt. So the model answers from *your* data (policies, catalogue, tickets), not its training memory. The pipeline:

1. Cut documents into chunks.
2. Turn each chunk into an embedding and store it.
3. Turn the question into an embedding.
4. Fetch the top-k closest chunks, optionally re-rank them.
5. Generate the answer, with citations.

RAG reduces **hallucination** (confidently made-up answers). It keeps answers fresh without retraining.

**(7) Vector databases.** These stores hold embeddings. They answer one question fast: "which vectors are nearest to this one?" They also filter by metadata, such as category, seller or language. Options include dedicated engines (Milvus, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate). There are also add-ons like pgvector, and vector fields in Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. The trade-off is **recall versus latency versus memory**.

**(16) HNSW.** Hierarchical Navigable Small World comes from Malkov and Yashunin's paper. It is the most widely used **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** index. "Approximate" means it may miss a few true matches, in exchange for speed.

It builds layered graphs. Sparse top layers make long jumps. Dense bottom layers do fine search. Think highway first, then local roads. Search is roughly logarithmic. Recall is high, often 95-99 percent. You tune it with parameters **M** and **efSearch**. The cost is RAM.

### Step 3: Agents

**(1) How AI agents work.** An agent is an LLM in a loop:

1. Read the goal and context.
2. Decide an action, often a **tool call** (a structured request such as `get_order(id)`).
3. Run it, and add the result to the context.
4. Repeat until done or a limit is hit.

The model plans; ordinary code executes.

**(3) MCP.** Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol in late 2024. It has since been adopted widely. It standardises how an AI app connects to tools and data. An **MCP server** exposes tools, resources and prompts. Any MCP-capable client can use them. So N apps times M integrations becomes N plus M.

**(8) Designing an AI agent.** The engineering choices: which tools and permissions, step and cost budgets, and when a human must approve (refunds above a threshold). Add guardrails on inputs and outputs, error handling, and **observability** (tracing every step). Start with the simplest design that works.

**(10) Agentic patterns.** These are reusable shapes:

- **Prompt chaining**: fixed steps in order.
- **Routing**: classify, then send to a specialist.
- **Parallelisation**: run parts at the same time.
- **Orchestrator-workers**: a lead splits work among helpers.
- **Evaluator-optimiser**: one call drafts, another critiques.
- **ReAct**: reason, act, observe.
- **Reflection**: the model reviews its own work.

Anthropic's "Building effective agents" guidance stresses one point. A fixed **workflow** is often better than a free-roaming agent.

**(9) Multi-agent architecture.** Several agents with their own roles and contexts, coordinated by a supervisor, a hierarchy or peer hand-offs. It helps when sub-tasks are separable or need different tools. The cost is more tokens, more latency and more ways to fail.

**(11) Agent memory, state and consistency.** **Short-term memory** is the current context. **Long-term memory** is stored facts and summaries, retrieved later. **State** is where a multi-step task stands, like "step 3 of 5, refund pending". The consistency problems are normal distributed-systems problems. You need **idempotent** tool calls (safe to repeat). You need checkpoints so a crashed agent resumes. And never trust stale memory over the **system of record** (the real database).

**(18) A2A protocol.** Google announced Agent2Agent in 2025 and moved it to the Linux Foundation. It lets agents from different teams or vendors find each other through an **"agent card"**. They can then delegate tasks and exchange results. Short version: **MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects an agent to other agents.**

**(19) AI research agents.** Long-running agents that plan a question, search many sources, take notes and write a cited report, often with an orchestrator spawning parallel sub-agents. They stress every agent concept.

**(15) Designing a personal AI chat assistant.** A system-design case study using nearly everything: streaming replies, chat storage, long-term memory, RAG over user files, tools, safety and per-user cost control.

### Step 4: Quality and adaptation

**(13) LLM evals.** Tests for output that can change run to run. They include golden datasets with expected answers. They include code checks, like "is this valid JSON?" or "was the right tool chosen?". They include **LLM-as-judge** (a model scores answers with a rubric), human review and live metrics such as resolution rate and escalations. Evals gate every prompt, model or retrieval change. They are the AI version of a regression suite.

**(12) Fine-tuning.** Continue training on your own examples to change behaviour: format, tone, domain words, or one narrow task. **LoRA** and similar methods train small add-on weights, not the whole model. Rule of thumb: **RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour.**

**(14) Reinforcement learning.** Training by reward, not copying. **RLHF** (RL from human feedback) uses a reward model trained on human preferences. **DPO** optimises preferences directly. RL with **verifiable rewards** (tests pass, maths is correct) drives today's reasoning models. Most product teams use RL-trained models. They rarely run RL themselves.

**(17) Vertical small LLMs.** Small models, roughly 1-15 billion **parameters** (learned numbers), built for one domain or task. They are often distilled or fine-tuned from larger ones. They are cheaper and faster, and can be self-hosted for data control. But they are weaker at open-ended reasoning. So they suit high-volume narrow tasks.

### Step 5: Production scale

**(6) Scaling an AI app to 1M users.** Use the usual playbook plus AI-specific levers:

- Rate limits and quotas per user.
- **Model routing**: cheap model first, large model only when needed.
- **Prompt caching** and semantic response caching.
- Batching, streaming, and fallbacks across providers.
- Async queues for long jobs.
- Cost and latency tracking per request.

**GPU or API cost, not CPU, is usually the binding constraint.**

### How the layers connect

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Model fundamentals] --> B[Context engineering]
  C[Vector DB and HNSW] --> D[RAG]
  D --> B
  F[MCP tools] --> E[Agent loop]
  B --> E
  E --> G[Multi agent and A2A]
  H[Evals and fine tuning] --> E
  G --> I[Scale to 1M users]
```

Fundamentals feed retrieval and context. Context feeds the agent loop. Evals measure everything. Scale wraps it all.

### Suggested learning order

1. LLM concepts, then context engineering. Everything else assumes these.
2. Embeddings in practice: vector databases, HNSW, then RAG.
3. How agents work, MCP, agentic patterns, designing an agent.
4. LLM evals. Learn them early; they change how you judge everything after.
5. Memory and state, multi-agent, A2A, research agents.
6. Fine-tuning, RL, vertical small LLMs.
7. The two system-design capstones: personal chat assistant and scaling to 1M users.

### What matters most at Director level

A Director is judged on **choices and trade-offs**, not on deriving attention. Prioritise these:

- **RAG versus fine-tuning versus small models**: cost, freshness, control.
- **Evals** as the release gate.
- **Agent design** with guardrails and human approval.
- **Scaling and unit economics**, like cost per resolved ticket.
- **MCP and A2A** as platform standards, so many teams plug in without custom integrations.

Know HNSW and RL well enough for two sentences each.

## A worked example

Back to Shreya and her shoe search on sale week. The assistant has a **16k-token** context window budget. Press Play.

```anim
{"title": "One question through all five layers", "w": 680, "h": 400, "intro": "Shreya asks a shopping assistant for running shoes. Watch each layer add its piece. Press Play.",
 "nodes": [
  {"id": "user", "label": "Shreya", "sub": "shopper", "x": 10, "y": 40, "w": 100, "h": 44, "kind": "user"},
  {"id": "router", "label": "Small model", "sub": "router", "x": 10, "y": 170, "w": 110, "h": 48, "kind": "service"},
  {"id": "vdb", "label": "Vector DB", "sub": "HNSW index", "x": 10, "y": 300, "w": 110, "h": 48, "kind": "db"},
  {"id": "ctx", "label": "Context window, 16k tokens", "x": 150, "y": 172, "w": 380, "h": 44, "kind": "log", "cw": 66},
  {"id": "mcp", "label": "MCP tools", "sub": "delivery, offers", "x": 150, "y": 300, "w": 130, "h": 48, "kind": "service"},
```

1. **Request.** Shreya's text becomes tokens, within the 16k budget (concept 4).
2. **Routing.** A small vertical model labels the intent "product discovery", not "order support" (patterns 10, small LLMs 17).
3. **Retrieval.** The query is embedded. It is searched against catalogue and review embeddings in a vector store with an HNSW index. Filters keep price and pincode delivery in range (7, 16). The top 20 hits are re-ranked to 5 and passed in as context (RAG, 2).
4. **Tools.** The agent calls `check_delivery(pincode, sku)` and `get_offers(sku)`. Internal MCP servers, owned by the logistics and pricing teams, expose them (3, 1).
5. **Context assembly.** System rules, Shreya's shoe size from long-term memory, five products, delivery results and the output format are packed into the window (5, 11).
6. **Answer.** The large model writes a short comparison with links, streamed to the app. The loop is capped at 6 steps and a budget of ₹0.50 per request.
7. **Follow-up.** Shreya asks to return last month's pair. A support agent takes over through an A2A hand-off. It has its own tools and a human approval step for refunds above a threshold (18, 9, 8).
8. **Quality.** Every prompt or model change runs against **2,000 golden queries**. An LLM judge scores them, and checks confirm prices and delivery dates match the tools (13). Low-scoring answer styles become fine-tuning data for the router (12). The base models were already preference-tuned with RL by their providers (14).
9. **Scale.** On sale night, semantic caching serves repeated questions. **80 percent of traffic stays on the small model.** The large model is rate-limited per user, and there is a fallback provider (6). The design grows into a personal assistant (15), and an offline research agent (19) writes weekly competitor-pricing reports with it.

That one feature touches all 19 concepts.

## Common misconceptions

- **"A bigger context window removes the need for RAG."** Long contexts cost more and run slower. Models still miss facts buried in the middle. Retrieval keeps the window small and relevant.
- **"Fine-tuning is how you teach the model our catalogue."** Facts change daily. Fine-tuning bakes in a snapshot. Use RAG for knowledge and fine-tuning for behaviour and format.
- **"Every AI feature should be an agent."** Agents add latency, cost and unpredictability. A fixed workflow is often better.
- **"MCP and A2A compete."** They work together: agent-to-tool versus agent-to-agent.
- **"Evals are a final QA step."** They are the ongoing regression suite. Without them, you cannot safely change a prompt, a model or a chunking strategy.
- **"Vector search is exact."** HNSW is approximate. It trades a little recall for big speed gains, so you must measure recall.

## How to say it in an interview

*"I think of AI engineering as five layers. At the bottom is the model. It predicts tokens and uses attention over a limited context window. So the core skill is context engineering: deciding what goes into that window. Second is retrieval. RAG over a vector database, usually with an HNSW index, lets the model answer from our data, not stale training memory. Third is agents: an LLM in a loop calling tools. MCP is the standard for tools, and A2A is the standard for agent hand-offs. Fourth is quality. Evals gate every change. When prompting and retrieval aren't enough, I fine-tune, use RL-tuned models, or move narrow high-volume tasks to small models. Fifth is scale: routing, caching, rate limits and fallbacks, because cost per request is the real limit. My default is the simplest design that passes evals. I add complexity only where the metrics justify it."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *RAG or fine-tuning for a support bot?* RAG for policies and order data, because they change. Fine-tune only if tone, format or classification stays poor after good prompting. Prove it with evals.
- *When would you go multi-agent?* When sub-tasks need different tools, permissions or context, and can run independently. Otherwise one agent with good tools is cheaper and easier to debug.
- *How do you control cost at 1M users?* Send most traffic to small models. Cache prompts and answers. Cap steps and tokens per request. Track cost per resolved outcome as a business metric.
- *How do you know the assistant is safe to ship?* Offline golden sets, adversarial tests, fact checks against tools, a canary rollout with live metrics, and human review of a sample.

## Key takeaways

- The 19 concepts form **five layers**: fundamentals, retrieval, agents, quality and adaptation, scale.
- The model only knows its **context window**. **Context engineering** is the central skill.
- **RAG plus a vector DB with HNSW** brings fresh, private knowledge into that window.
- An **agent is an LLM in a loop with tools**. **MCP** standardises tools; **A2A** standardises agent-to-agent.
- Prefer **simple workflows** over free agents until evals show you need more.
- **Evals** are the release gate for every change.
- **RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour**, small vertical models for cheap narrow tasks.
- At scale, **cost per request** drives the design: routing, caching, limits, fallbacks.

## Check yourself

1. Your support bot gives outdated return-policy answers. Do you fine-tune, add RAG, or enlarge the context window, and why?
   Answer: Add or fix RAG over the current policy documents. The problem is stale knowledge, which retrieval solves cheaply. Fine-tuning would bake in another snapshot, and a bigger window does not help if the right document is not retrieved.
2. What is the difference between MCP and A2A, in one sentence each?
   Answer: MCP is a standard for connecting an AI app or agent to tools and data sources. A2A is a standard for one agent to discover, delegate to and exchange results with another agent.
3. Which three concepts would you put first on a roadmap for a shopping assistant before a festive sale, and why?
   Answer: RAG over the catalogue for accurate grounded answers, LLM evals as a release gate so changes do not regress, and scaling practices like routing and caching so sale-night traffic is affordable. Agents and fine-tuning can follow once these work.
4. In Shreya's example, why does a small model see the request before the large model?
   Answer: It is a cheap router. It classifies intent, so most traffic, about 80 percent on sale night, never needs the expensive large model, and order-support questions go straight to the support agent.

question: LLM concepts deep dive: what are tokens, embeddings, attention and context windows, and how does an LLM generate text?
answer:
## The short answer

A **large language model (LLM)** is a neural network trained to do one thing. Given some text, it **predicts the next token**. Chat, code, summaries and tool use all come from repeating that one prediction in a loop.

- **Tokens** are the pieces of text the model reads and writes. A **tokenizer** cuts text into tokens, usually with a subword method called **BPE (byte-pair encoding)**. One token is about 4 characters of English. Indian-language text often needs **several times more tokens** for the same meaning.
- **Embeddings** turn each token into a list of numbers (a few thousand of them). Similar meanings get similar numbers.
- **Transformer blocks**, stacked dozens of times, refine those numbers. Their key part is **self-attention**: each token looks at every earlier token and decides what matters. It uses **queries, keys and values (Q, K, V)**. Its cost grows **quadratically** (with the square of the input length).
- **Generation** goes one token at a time. The model gives a probability to every possible next token. A picker **samples** one, shaped by **temperature** and **top-p**. The token is appended, and the loop repeats. A **KV cache** saves past work.
- The **context window** is the most tokens the model can see at once, prompt plus output. Models use the **middle** of long contexts less reliably.
- Training has stages: **pretraining**, **instruction tuning** and **preference tuning such as RLHF**. **Hallucinations** happen because the model is trained for plausible text, not checked truth.
- **Cost and latency scale with tokens.**

## The intuition

Shreya's order is late. She types into a Flipkart-like app, in Hinglish: "Mera order abhi tak nahi aaya, refund kab milega?" ("My order hasn't come yet, when will I get my refund?"). A support assistant replies in a second. What happened inside?

Think of a hugely well-read **autocomplete**. It is like your phone keyboard, but it has read much of the internet. It considers thousands of earlier words at once.

- **Token**: a Lego brick of text. Common words are one brick ("order"). Rare words are several ("re", "fund", "able"). The model never sees letters, only brick numbers.
- **Tokenizer**: cuts text into bricks. Each brick has a number from a fixed **vocabulary** of 50,000 to 250,000 entries.
- **Embedding**: a GPS coordinate for meaning. "Kurta" sits near "shirt", far from "invoice".
- **Attention**: a meeting. Each word asks a question (its **query**). Earlier words wear name tags (their **keys**). Each word collects notes (the **values**) from words whose tags match its question. In "the phone I returned last week was refunded", the word "refunded" pays most attention to "phone" and "returned".
- **Context window**: the size of the desk. Instructions, history, documents and the answer so far must all fit. Anything off the desk does not exist for the model.
- **Sampling**: the model does not pick "the" answer. It rolls a weighted die over possible next tokens. **Temperature** controls how lopsided the die is.
- **Hallucination**: a fluent student bluffing in an exam, because sounding right was rewarded.

## How it actually works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Text prompt] --> B[Tokenizer]
  B --> C[Embeddings plus position]
  C --> D[Transformer blocks]
  D --> E[Probabilities for next token]
  E --> F[Sample one token]
  F --> G{Stop token or limit}
  G -- no --> D
  G -- yes --> H[Text reply]
```

### 1. Tokenization and BPE

**Byte-pair encoding** starts with single bytes or characters. It finds the most frequent neighbouring pair in the training text and merges it into a new token. It repeats until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Frequent strings like "ing" or " delivery" become single tokens. Rare strings stay split.

Two results matter in production:

- **English is cheap.** Tokenizer training text is mostly English, so English words got merged into whole tokens.
- **Indian languages cost more.** Devanagari, Tamil and other Indic scripts use 3 bytes per character in UTF-8 (the standard text encoding). They were also rare when merges were learned. So a Hindi or Tamil sentence can need **2 to 5 times** the tokens of its English version, sometimes more with older tokenizers. That means higher cost, higher latency, and less room in the window. Newer tokenizers with bigger vocabularies have narrowed the gap. Exact ratios **depend on the model**, so measure with your own data (for example with OpenAI's open-source tiktoken library).

### 2. Embeddings

Each token number picks one row of a learned **embedding matrix**. Its size is vocabulary size times model width, for example 128,000 x 4,096. The row starts random. Training tunes it so tokens used in similar places get similar vectors. These are internal. The **embedding models** used for RAG search are separate models that give one vector per document.

### 3. Position

Attention alone treats input as an unordered bag. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look alike. So models add **position information**. The 2017 paper *Attention Is All You Need* (Vaswani et al.) added fixed sine and cosine patterns. Most current open models use **RoPE (rotary position embeddings)**. RoPE rotates query and key vectors by an angle based on position, so attention reflects **relative distance**.

### 4. A transformer block

The vectors pass through a stack of identical **blocks**, roughly 30 to 120+ in modern models. Each block does three things:

1. **Self-attention**: mix in information from other tokens.
2. **Feed-forward network (MLP)**: process each token's vector alone. Much stored knowledge is thought to live here.
3. **Residual connections and normalisation** around both. These keep training stable in deep stacks.

### 5. Self-attention and its quadratic cost

For each token, the block makes three vectors using learned weights:

- **Query Q**: what am I looking for?
- **Key K**: what do I contain?
- **Value V**: what will I pass on?

Then, in plain words:

1. Score every token against every token: Q times K, divided by the square root of the vector size.
2. Hide future tokens. A token may only look backwards (this is called **causal** masking).
3. Turn each row of scores into weights that add up to 1 (**softmax**).
4. Blend the values using those weights.

This runs as **multi-head attention**, for example 32 heads. Each head learns a different relationship. Watch one head work on a short sentence:

The score table is **n x n** for n tokens. That is why attention is **quadratic**: doubling the input roughly **quadruples** attention compute. Fixes include **FlashAttention** (same result, far less memory traffic), **grouped-query attention** (several query heads share one set of keys and values, to save memory), and sliding-window or sparse attention in some models.

### 6. Next-token prediction and sampling

After the last block, the final vector is scored against the whole vocabulary. That gives **logits**: one raw score per token. Softmax turns them into probabilities. Then the picker chooses:

- **Greedy**: always take the top token.
- **Temperature T**: divide logits by T before softmax. T below 1 sharpens the odds: safer, more repetitive. T above 1 flattens them: more varied, more errors. T near 0 is close to greedy.
- **Top-k**: keep only the k most likely tokens.
- **Top-p (nucleus)**: keep the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, say 0.9. Then sample among them. It adapts: confident steps keep few options, uncertain steps keep many.

Use low temperature for extraction and JSON. Use moderate temperature for marketing copy.

### 7. Prefill, decode and the KV cache

Serving has two phases:

- **Prefill**: process the whole prompt in one parallel pass. It is compute-heavy but fast per token. It sets the **time to first token**.
- **Decode**: make one token at a time. Each new token needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens. So servers keep them in a **KV cache** instead of recomputing. Decode is limited by **memory bandwidth**. That is why output tokens are slower and usually priced **3 to 5 times** higher than input tokens.

The KV cache grows with context length and batch size. A long conversation can take gigabytes. That limits how many users one GPU can serve. **Prompt caching**, offered by API vendors, reuses prefill work for a repeated start of the prompt, such as a long system prompt. It cuts cost and latency for that part.

### 8. Context windows and their limits

In 2026, frontier windows run from about 128K to 1M or more tokens; check each model's docs. The window holds **system prompt + history + retrieved documents + tool results + output**. Limits beyond the hard number:

- **Lost in the middle**: Liu et al.'s 2023 paper showed models find facts best near the **start or end** of a long context, worse in the middle. Newer models are better. But "needle in a haystack" tests overstate real reasoning over long inputs.
- **Cost and latency** grow with every token, on every call.
- **Distraction**: irrelevant context lowers accuracy. The right 5,000 tokens usually beat 500,000. That is the case for **RAG** (fetching only relevant documents).

### 9. Training in three stages

| Stage | Data | What it learns |
|---|---|---|
| **Pretraining** | Trillions of tokens of web, books, code | Language, facts, patterns; a "base model" that continues text |
| **Instruction tuning (SFT)** | Tens of thousands to millions of prompt and ideal-answer pairs | Follow instructions, chat format, tool-call format |
| **Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO, RL on verifiable tasks)** | Human or AI rankings of answers; tasks with checkable answers | Helpfulness, safety, tone; reasoning in newer "thinking" models |

**RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback)** was popularised by OpenAI's InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022). It trains a **reward model** on human comparisons. Then it tunes the LLM to score well on it. The later stages mostly shape behaviour. They do not add much knowledge.

### 10. Why hallucinations happen

- The goal is a **plausible next word**, not truth. A confident wrong answer can look as plausible as a right one.
- **Rare facts**, like one seller's return policy or a SKU code, were seen rarely or never. The model fills the gap.
- **Knowledge cutoff**: anything after training is unknown unless it is in the context.
- **Scoring habits**: OpenAI's 2025 paper *Why Language Models Hallucinate* argues that tests which score guessing above "I don't know" teach models to guess.
- **Sampling** can pick one wrong token that derails the rest.

Fixes: ground answers in fetched data (RAG), use tools for facts, allow "I don't know", and check outputs against the system of record.

### 11. Cost = tokens

Cost = input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price, minus the discount on cached input tokens. Levers: shorter prompts, prompt caching, smaller models for easy steps, capped output, and batch APIs for offline jobs.

## A worked example

**Shreya's Hinglish support chat during a festive sale.** Timing numbers are illustrative.

1. **The prompt.** The app builds about **4,000 input tokens**: a 2,000-token **system prompt** (role, policies, tone, JSON tool format), the last 6 chat turns (900 tokens), and **tool results** from the order service (1,100 tokens: status, promised date, refund rules for this category).
2. **Tokenization.** The team measured that Hindi-script replies cost about **2.5x** the tokens of English on their model. So they budget Hindi-script chats separately.
3. **Prefill.** The system prompt is the same for every chat. It sits first and hits the vendor's **prompt cache**. Only the changing 2,000 tokens are fully processed. Time to first token drops from about 900 ms to about 400 ms.
4. **Attention at work.** While writing "aapka refund", attention focuses on the tool line "refund_eta: 3 business days after pickup" and the policy text. It ignores older turns about a different order.
5. **Decoding.** Temperature **0.2** and top-p 0.9, because this is factual. The model first emits a structured tool call to check pickup status. Then it writes a 120-token reply. The KV cache keeps each step cheap.
6. **Guardrails.** The reply may only quote dates found in tool results. A validator checks every date and amount against the order record. If one fails, the reply is regenerated or sent to a human agent.
7. **Context management.** After 20 turns, older turns are summarised into 300 tokens. The policy and latest tool results stay near the start and end, away from the lost-in-the-middle zone.
8. **Cost at sale scale.** About 4,150 tokens per turn, 3 turns, **2 million conversations a day**. Caching the 2,000-token prefix cuts the input bill a lot, depending on the vendor's discount. Sending simple "where is my order" questions to a smaller model cuts it further.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The model looks up facts in a database."** It has no lookup. It rebuilds answers from patterns in its weights. For reliable facts, put them in the context or call a tool.
- **"Tokens are words."** They are word pieces. A word may be one to several tokens. Token counts for the same meaning vary widely across languages, which changes cost.
- **"A 1M-token window means the model uses all of it equally well."** Recall and reasoning drop on long inputs, especially in the middle. Every token also costs money and time.
- **"Temperature 0 makes the model correct and fully deterministic."** It makes it less random, not more accurate. Serving can still cause small run-to-run differences.
- **"RLHF teaches the model new knowledge."** Mostly it shapes behaviour: helpfulness, refusals, format. Knowledge comes mainly from pretraining, or from what you supply at runtime.
- **"The next model will remove hallucination."** Rates fall with better training and grounding. But a system that writes plausible text will sometimes be wrong. Design for it and verify.

## How to say it in an interview

*"An LLM is a next-token predictor. A subword tokenizer like BPE splits text into tokens. Tokens are also the billing unit, and Indian languages often take several times more tokens than English for the same meaning. Each token becomes an embedding plus position information, then flows through dozens of transformer blocks. The core of each block is self-attention. Every token makes a query, compares it with the keys of earlier tokens, and blends their values. That is why cost grows with the square of the length. The output is a probability for every token. We sample with temperature and top-p, append, and repeat, with a KV cache so past tokens aren't recomputed. The context window is a hard limit and a soft one, because models use the middle less reliably. So I prefer retrieval over stuffing. Pretraining gives knowledge; instruction tuning and RLHF give behaviour. Hallucination comes from training for plausibility, so I ground answers in our systems and validate them. As a leader, I treat tokens as the unit of cost and latency."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *Why are output tokens dearer than input tokens?* Input is processed in one parallel prefill pass. Output comes one token at a time, each step reading the whole KV cache. That is memory-bound and holds the GPU longer.
- *How would you reduce hallucinations in a support bot?* Fetch order and policy data with tools. Tell the model to answer only from that. Use low temperature. Check numbers and dates against the source. Escalate when checks fail.
- *Why not use the biggest window available?* Cost and latency grow with tokens, attention quality drops on long noisy input, and irrelevant context lowers accuracy. Retrieval plus summaries usually gives better answers for less money.

## Key takeaways

- An LLM is a **next-token predictor** run in a loop.
- **Tokens** are word pieces from BPE-style tokenizers. They are the **unit of cost and latency**, and Indian languages often need **several times more**.
- **Embeddings plus position** feed **transformer blocks**. **Self-attention (Q, K, V)** lets tokens use each other, at **quadratic** cost.
- **Temperature and top-p** shape sampling: low for facts and JSON, higher for creative text.
- **Prefill vs decode** and the **KV cache** explain time to first token and why output costs more.
- **Context windows** have hard and soft limits. Selective context beats stuffing.
- **Pretraining** gives knowledge; **instruction tuning and RLHF** give behaviour.
- **Hallucination** is built in. **Ground, cite and validate** in production.

## Check yourself

1. Your Tamil support flow costs far more per chat than the English one, with identical logic. What is the likely cause, and what would you do?
   Answer: Tokenization. Tamil script splits into many more tokens than English with most tokenizers. Measure tokens per language, consider a model with a more Indic-friendly tokenizer, cache stable prompt prefixes, keep system prompts in English where acceptable, and budget per language.
2. Doubling a prompt from 50K to 100K tokens made prefill much slower than double. Why?
   Answer: Self-attention compares every token with every earlier token, so its work grows with the square of length. Doubling length roughly quadruples the attention part, on top of linear costs like the KV cache.
3. An attribute-extraction job returns slightly different, sometimes invented colours across runs. Which two changes help?
   Answer: Lower the temperature to near 0 with a fixed JSON format to cut randomness. Then restrict answers to values in the input or an allowed list, with a validator that rejects anything not in the source.
4. In Shreya's chat, why does time to first token drop from about 900 ms to about 400 ms?
   Answer: The 2,000-token system prompt is identical for every chat and placed first, so prompt caching reuses its prefill work. Only the changing 2,000 tokens need full prefill.

question: Why does an AI chatbot give a different answer each time you ask the same question? Temperature, top-p and randomness explained.
answer:
## The short answer

A large language model (**LLM**) does not look up one fixed answer. It writes its reply **one token at a time**. A token is a word or a piece of a word. At every step, the model gives a **probability to every possible next token**. Then something must **pick** one.

- If the picker always takes the most likely token, that is **greedy decoding**. The answer is (almost) repeatable.
- Most chatbots instead **sample**: they roll a weighted dice. A 50% token wins about half the time. A 25% token wins about a quarter of the time.

One different pick early on changes everything after it. So you get a different answer.

Three knobs control the dice roll:

- **Temperature** reshapes the probabilities. Low (0 to 0.3) lets the top choice dominate: focused and repeatable. High (1.2 and above) flattens them: more varied, more creative, more mistakes.
- **Top-k** keeps only the k most likely tokens before rolling.
- **Top-p (nucleus sampling)** keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p, say 0.9. It drops the long tail of weird options.

Even **temperature 0** is **not always identical bit for bit**. **Floating-point rounding** (tiny maths rounding on chips) and server **batching** can change it. Use **low temperature plus validation** for support, code and JSON. Use more randomness for creative text. **Seeds** help repeatability. **Self-consistency** (sample several answers, then vote) turns randomness into reliability.

## The intuition

Shreya asks a Flipkart-like support bot: "When do I get my UPI refund?" Her friend asks the exact same question. They get different replies. Why?

Think of a Swiggy delivery partner riding home. At every junction, the map app shows how often riders take each road: left 50%, straight 25%, right 15%, others 10%.

- A **greedy** rider always takes the most popular road. Same start, same route, every day.
- A **sampling** rider picks roads in proportion to popularity. Most days she goes left. Some days, straight. One different turn at the first junction changes the whole trip. Yet every single choice was sensible.
- **Temperature** is the rider's mood. Low: "just take the popular road". High: "let's explore, every road looks about as good".
- **Top-k** and **top-p** are rules like "never take a road fewer than 5% of riders use". They stop her wandering into a dead end.

Terms used in this answer:

- **Token**: a chunk of text the model reads and writes. (The app's LLM basics answer covers tokens, embeddings and attention.)
- **Logit**: the raw score the model gives each possible next token, before it becomes a probability.
- **Softmax**: the formula that turns logits into probabilities that add up to 1.
- **Decoding**: the step that turns probabilities into one chosen token.
- **Sampling**: choosing randomly, weighted by probability.
- **Deterministic**: the same input always gives exactly the same output.

## How it actually works

### Step 1: The model gives a probability for every next token

A shopping assistant is completing: "The best time to buy a phone on a Flipkart-like site is during the ...". The model scores every token in its vocabulary, often 50,000 to 200,000 of them. Here are the top five, with illustrative numbers:

| Next token | Probability at temperature 1.0 |
|---|---|
| sale | 0.50 |
| festive | 0.25 |
| weekend | 0.15 |
| night | 0.07 |
| monsoon | 0.03 |

The model itself is deterministic. Same input, same table. **The randomness comes from the picker.**

### Step 2: Greedy vs sampling

- **Greedy**: always take the top token, "sale". Repeatable, but often bland. Long outputs can get stuck in loops.
- **Sampling**: draw a random number between 0 and 1. From 0 to 0.50, pick "sale". From 0.50 to 0.75, "festive". And so on. Over 100 runs, you would see "sale" about 50 times and "festive" about 25 times.

A 300-token answer is 300 dice rolls in a row. So two runs rarely match word for word.

```mermaid
    B --> C[Divide by temperature]
    C --> D[Softmax to probabilities]
    D --> E[Top k or top p filter]
    E --> F[Pick one token]
    F --> G{End of answer}
    G -- no --> A
    G -- yes --> H[Return reply]
```

```anim
  {"say": "Back at 1.0, add top-p 0.9. Sale, festive and weekend add up to 0.90, so only those three stay.", "highlight": ["topp"], "mark": [{"node": "probs", "index": 2}]},
  {"say": "Night and monsoon are dropped. The three survivors are rescaled to about 0.56, 0.28 and 0.17. Nonsense picks are now impossible.", "highlight": ["probs"], "remove": [{"node": "probs", "index": 3}, {"node": "probs", "index": 4}]}
 ]}
```

### Step 3: Temperature reshapes the odds

Temperature **T** divides the logits before softmax. Probability is proportional to exp(logit / T). In maths terms, this equals raising each probability to the power 1/T, then rescaling so they add to 1. Same table, three temperatures:

| Token | T = 0.2 | T = 1.0 | T = 1.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| sale | 0.967 | 0.50 | 0.40 |
| festive | 0.030 | 0.25 | 0.25 |
| weekend | 0.002 | 0.15 | 0.18 |
| night | ~0 | 0.07 | 0.11 |
| monsoon | ~0 | 0.03 | 0.06 |

- **T = 0.2**: "sale" wins about 97 times in 100. Nearly greedy.
- **T = 1.0**: the model's own odds, unchanged.
- **T = 1.5**: flatter. "Monsoon", an odd choice, now has double its original chance.
- **T = 0** is a special case. Dividing by zero is undefined, so systems just take the top token (greedy).

Temperature never changes the ranking. It adds no knowledge. It only changes **how often lower-ranked options win**.

### Step 4: Top-k and top-p cut off the tail

With 100,000 tokens, tiny probabilities add up. At high temperature, the dice sometimes lands on nonsense. Two filters stop this.

- **Top-k**: keep only the k most likely tokens, then rescale. With k = 2: sale 0.667, festive 0.333. The catch: k is fixed. It is too loose when the model is sure, and too tight when many words fit.
- **Top-p (nucleus sampling)**: sort tokens by probability. Keep adding until the total reaches p. With p = 0.9 at T = 1.0: sale 0.50 + festive 0.25 + weekend 0.15 = 0.90. Keep those three, rescaled to about 0.56, 0.28 and 0.17. Drop "night" and "monsoon". At T = 1.5, the same p = 0.9 needs four tokens, because the odds are flatter. **Top-p adapts**: few options when the model is confident, more when it is not.

The usual order is: apply temperature, then top-k and/or top-p, then sample. Defaults vary by provider. Many guides suggest changing temperature **or** top-p, not both at once. Then you can tell which knob caused a change.

### Step 5: Why temperature 0 is still not always identical

People are surprised when temperature 0 gives slightly different answers. The reasons:

- **Floating-point maths is not exactly associative.** On a GPU, (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) in the last few bits. Big sums are split across thousands of parallel threads, and the order can vary.
- **Batching.** A hosted model serves many users at once, grouped into a **batch**. The batch size and its neighbours can change which internal maths routines (**kernels**) run and how sums are split. So the logits for *your* request shift by a tiny amount.
- **Near ties.** Usually those tiny shifts do not matter. But say two tokens are nearly tied, 0.4001 vs 0.3999. A rounding wobble flips the winner. From that token on, the whole answer changes.
- **Other moving parts**: model updates, hidden system prompt changes, different hardware.

So temperature 0 means **"as repeatable as practical"**, not a guarantee. Bit-exact results need special engineering: deterministic kernels, fixed batching, pinned versions. That usually costs speed.

### Step 6: Seeds

The dice rolls are **pseudo-random**. They come from a starting number called a **seed**. Same seed, same rolls. Some APIs and most self-hosted stacks accept a seed. That makes sampled outputs **mostly reproducible** for debugging and tests. The temperature-0 caveats still apply. Providers often call seeds **best effort**.

### Step 7: Self-consistency, using randomness on purpose

Some questions have one right answer, like a refund amount or a category. For these, **sample several answers (say 5) at moderate temperature and take a majority vote**. Wrong paths tend to make different mistakes. Correct paths tend to agree. This often beats one greedy answer on reasoning tasks, at about 5x the cost.

The agreement level is also a **free confidence signal**. 5 out of 5 agree: ship it. A 2-2-1 split: escalate to a human. (The app's LLM evals answer covers how to measure whether such tricks really help.)

### Choosing settings: creativity vs consistency

| Use case | Suggested setting | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Support answers, policy questions | T 0 to 0.3 | Same question, same policy answer; fewer invented details |
| Code generation | T 0 to 0.2 | One wrong token breaks the code |
| JSON / structured extraction | T 0 plus a schema or constrained output | Format must parse every time |
| Product descriptions, ad copy | T 0.7 to 1.0, top-p 0.9 to 0.95 | Variety is the point |
| Brainstorming names, festive taglines | T 1.0 to 1.2 | Want unusual options, a human filters |
| Reasoning with voting | T 0.5 to 0.8, 5 samples | Need diversity for the vote to help |

These are illustrative starting points. Test on your own data.

## A worked example

A Flipkart-like marketplace runs a support bot and a seller-content tool during its festive sale.

**Problem 1: inconsistent refund answers.** Shreya and her friend both ask: "The seller cancelled my order, when do I get my UPI refund?" At temperature 0.9, the bot tells Shreya "2 to 4 business days". It tells her friend "24 hours". Both replies are fluent. One is wrong. Screenshots go viral.

The fixes:

1. **Drop temperature to 0.1** for the support flow. Keep top-p at 1.0, since there is no need to turn both knobs.
2. **Ground the answer.** The refund timeline comes from a policy document fetched for the question (the app's RAG answer covers this). The model copies a fact instead of guessing.
3. **Validate.** A check confirms any number of days in the reply matches the policy table. If not, the bot falls back to a templated answer.
4. **Log the seed and model version** with each chat, so a complaint can be replayed.

**Problem 2: the opposite complaint.** Sellers use a tool to write product titles and festive taglines. At temperature 0.1, every seller of a phone cover gets almost the same line: "Protect your phone in style this festive season". The team **raises temperature to 0.9 with top-p 0.95**. It makes 3 options per request and lets the seller pick. Variety goes up. A simple filter rejects any tagline that mentions a discount the seller did not offer.

**Problem 3: an attribute-extraction job.** A nightly job fills JSON records (brand, colour, size) from seller descriptions. At temperature 0, a few records in thousands still differ between reruns. These are near-ties, like "navy" vs "blue", flipping under batching. The fix has two parts. **Restrict colour to an allowed list.** For low-confidence fields, **run 3 samples and vote**. Disagreements go to human review. Cost stays small, because only uncertain fields are re-sampled. Watch it happen:

```anim

Agreement is also a confidence signal.", "send": [{"from": "votes", "to": "vote", "label": "2 navy, 1 blue", "color": "a"}, {"from": "vote", "to": "db", "label": "colour: navy", "color": "a"}], "highlight": ["vote"], "mark": [{"node": "votes", "index": 0}, {"node": "votes", "index": 1}]},
  {"say": "For another product the three samples all disagree. No majority, so a person decides instead of a guess.", "send": [{"from": "vote", "to": "human", "label": "No majority", "color": "d"}], "highlight": ["human"]},
  {"say": "Cost stays small. Only the uncertain fields are re-sampled; confident fields keep their single temperature-0 answer.", "highlight": ["ext", "vote"]}
```

The lesson: **one platform, three settings**. Each is chosen by what a wrong answer, or a boring one, costs.

## Common misconceptions

1. **"The model randomly makes things up, so it is unreliable by nature."** For a given input, the model's probabilities are fixed. Randomness is a decoding choice you control. Turn it down where consistency matters.
2. **"Temperature 0 guarantees identical output."** It removes the dice roll. But rounding, batching, hardware and silent model updates can still change the result. Treat it as near-deterministic and design for small variation.
3. **"Low temperature stops hallucinations."** It makes the model pick its top guess every time. If that guess is wrong, you get the same wrong answer every time. Fix hallucinations with grounding and validation. Temperature only reduces random drift.
4. **"Higher temperature makes the model smarter."** It only makes less likely tokens win more often. Past about 1.3 to 1.5, output usually becomes incoherent.
5. **"Top-p 0.9 means the answer is 90% accurate."** It means the picker keeps the top tokens covering 90% of the probability. It says nothing about correctness.

## How to say it in an interview

*"An LLM writes one token at a time. At each step it gives a probability for every possible next token, and a decoding step picks one. Always picking the top token is greedy decoding, and it is nearly repeatable. Most chat products sample instead, picking in proportion to probability. So one different early pick sends the whole answer down another path. Temperature reshapes the odds: low lets the top choice dominate, high flattens them for variety. Top-k and top-p cut off the long tail of unlikely tokens, and top-p adapts to how confident the model is. Even at temperature zero, outputs can vary slightly. GPU rounding and server batching cause tiny number shifts that can flip near-ties. So I choose settings per use case. Near zero plus schema validation for support, code and JSON. Higher temperature for copywriting and brainstorming. For answers with one right result, I can sample several times and vote, which also gives me a confidence signal."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- **Q: Temperature or top-p, which would you tune?** A: Usually one at a time. Temperature for overall focus vs variety. Top-p when you want variety but must avoid rare junk tokens. Changing both makes results hard to reason about.
- **Q: How do you make LLM tests reproducible?** A: Pin the model version. Use temperature 0 or a seed. Log the prompt and settings. Assert properties, like valid JSON and correct facts, not exact strings.
- **Q: When is self-consistency worth the cost?** A: For high-value, single-answer decisions, such as refund eligibility or fraud flags, where an error costs more than a few extra calls.

## Key takeaways

- The model gives **probabilities**. The **decoder** chooses, and that choice is where randomness enters.
- **Greedy** picks the top token. **Sampling** rolls a weighted dice at every token, so small early differences snowball.
- **Temperature** reshapes the odds: 0.2 is sharp, 1.0 is unchanged, 1.5 is flat. It never changes the ranking.
- **Top-k** keeps a fixed number of tokens. **Top-p** keeps a probability budget and adapts to confidence.
- **Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not guaranteed.** Rounding, batching and model updates can still cause drift.
- Use **low temperature plus grounding and validation** for support, code and JSON. Use **higher temperature** for creative text.
- **Seeds** help reproducibility on a best-effort basis. Log them with the model version and settings.
- **Self-consistency** (sample several, vote) turns randomness into accuracy and a confidence score.

## Check yourself

1. Using the table above, what happens to the chance of "monsoon" as temperature goes from 0.2 to 1.5, and why?
   Answer: It rises from almost 0 to about 6%. Higher temperature divides the logits by a bigger number. That shrinks the gaps between scores, so the odds flatten and low-ranked tokens win more often.
2. Your support bot gives the same wrong refund timeline every time at temperature 0. Will raising or lowering temperature fix it?
   Answer: No. Temperature 0 already picks the model's top guess every time; the guess itself is wrong. Ground the answer in the policy document and validate the number against the policy table.
3. At T = 1.0 with top-p = 0.9, which tokens from the example survive, and what are their new probabilities?
   Answer: Sale, festive and weekend (0.50 + 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.90). Rescaled, they become about 0.56, 0.28 and 0.17. Night and monsoon are dropped.
4. Why might two runs at temperature 0 on a hosted API still differ?
   Answer: The server batches your request with others and runs parallel GPU sums whose order can vary. Rounding shifts the logits slightly, and if two tokens are nearly tied, the winner can flip and the rest of the answer changes. Model or system-prompt updates can also change outputs.

question: Why do AI models confidently make things up, and how do you stop a customer-facing AI from inventing a refund policy?
answer:
## The short answer

A **hallucination** is when an AI model states something that sounds right but is false or unsupported. Examples: a made-up fact, a fake citation, a refund rule that doesn't exist.

It happens because a large language model (**LLM**) is trained to **predict plausible next words, not to check truth**. When it doesn't know, the most "plausible" next words are often a confident guess. Most of its training text is written confidently, so the guess sounds confident too.

You can't switch hallucination off inside the model. You **design the system around it**:

- **Ground** answers in real documents (**RAG**, retrieval-augmented generation) and require **citations**.
- Get **facts from tools**, not memory. Order status, refund eligibility and prices come from APIs.
- Give the model permission, with examples, to say **"I don't know"**. **Hand off to a human** when confidence is low.
- **Constrain outputs** (fixed fields, allowed values). Add a **verification step** before anything reaches the customer.
- **Measure** a hallucination rate with evals and production sampling. Track it like any other quality metric.

For a refund question, the rule is simple: **the bot never decides policy; it quotes policy and calls the refund system.**

## The intuition

Picture a very well-read new hire at a call centre, on day one. They have read millions of support chats, so they know exactly how an answer *sounds*.

Shreya calls: "Can I return a phone after 15 days?" The new hire doesn't know this company's rule. But they have seen thousands of return policies, and many say "30 days". So they answer smoothly: "Yes, you have 30 days." Nobody told them that guessing is worse than asking a supervisor.

That is a hallucination. The fixes for the human are obvious:

- **Give them the policy binder** (grounding).
- **Let them look up the order** (tools).
- **Tell them "let me check" is fine** (abstention).
- **Have a supervisor review risky answers** (verification).
- **Listen to a sample of calls** (evals).

Terms:

- **LLM**: a model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next **token** (a word or word piece). See the separate LLM basics answer.
- **Hallucination**: output not supported by the facts, or by the source the model was given.
- **Grounding**: giving the model trusted source text at answer time, and asking it to answer only from that.
- **RAG**: fetching relevant documents and putting them in the prompt (covered in its own answer).
- **Faithfulness**: whether every claim in the answer is supported by the given sources.
- **Abstention**: the model choosing not to answer ("I don't know", "let me connect you").
- **Tool call**: the model asking the app to run a function, such as `get_order_status`, and using the real result.

## How it actually works

### Step 1: Why models make things up

An LLM writes one token at a time. At each step it picks a likely next token, given everything so far. It has **no built-in "I checked this" signal**. "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days" is very likely text, whether or not it is true for *your* company.

Four common causes:

- **Gaps in training data.** The model never saw your refund policy. Or it saw an old version, or a rare fact only once. It fills the gap with the most typical pattern.
- **Pressure to answer.** Training often rewards helpful, complete answers. Many tests give no credit for "I don't know". So, on average, a guess scores better than abstaining. The model learns that **guessing pays**.
- **Long or noisy context.** With a long prompt (many documents, long chat history), the model can miss the key line. It can mix up two products, or blend an old policy with a new one.
- **Ambiguous prompts.** "What's the return window?" Which category, which seller, which date? The model picks one meaning and answers it confidently.

Confidence is the dangerous part. **The tone of the text says nothing about correctness.** The model writes fluently either way.

### Step 2: Types of hallucination

| Type | What it looks like | Support-bot example |
|---|---|---|
| **Factual** | A wrong fact stated as true | "Electronics have a 30-day return window" (real: 7 days) |
| **Unfaithful to source** | Contradicts or goes beyond the document it was given | Policy says "unused items only"; bot drops that condition |
| **Citation** | Invents a source, or cites a real one that doesn't say it | "As per policy section 4.2" (no such section) |
| **Tool-argument** | Makes up inputs to a function call | Calls `get_order("OD123456")` with an order ID the user never gave |
| **Action/state** | Claims something happened that didn't | "Your refund has been initiated" when no API was called |

The last two matter most for **agents** (AI that takes actions; see the AI agents answer). A made-up argument or a made-up "done" causes **real-world damage**, not just a wrong sentence.

Press Play to watch a bot with no safeguards produce three of these types in one chat:

```anim

  {"say": "The bot has no policy and no order data. All it has are patterns from millions of support chats.", "append": [{"node": "mem", "label": "30 days", "color": "e"}, {"node": "mem", "label": "3-5 days", "color": "e"}, {"node": "mem", "label": "Full refund", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["mem"]},
  {"say": "Many policies it saw say 30 days. So 30 days is the most plausible next text. Plausible, not checked.", "send": [{"from": "mem", "to": "llm", "label": "Sounds right: 30 days", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["mem"], "mark": [{"node": "mem", "index": 0}]},
  {"say": "Factual hallucination: it replies yes, 30 days, money in 3-5 days. The real rule is 7 days, replacement only.", "send": [{"from": "llm", "to": "user", "label": "Yes, 30 days!", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["user"]},
  {"say": "Tool-argument hallucination: it looks up order OD123456, an ID Shreya never gave.", "send": [{"from": "llm", "to": "orders", "label": "get_order(OD123456)", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["orders"]},
  {"say": "Action hallucination: it says your refund has been initiated. The refund API was never called.", "send": [{"from": "llm", "to": "user", "label": "Refund initiated", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["api"]},
  {"say": "Shreya screenshots the reply. Now the company must honour a policy it never had, or face an angry customer.", "send": [{"from": "user", "to": "shot", "label": "Screenshot", "color": "e"}], "highlight": ["shot"]}
 ]}
```

### Step 3: Stack the safeguards, layer by layer

No single fix is enough. You stack cheap layers. Each one catches what the previous one missed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Customer question] --> B[Classify intent]
  B --> C[Retrieve policy docs]
  B --> D[Call order tools]
  C --> E[LLM drafts answer]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Verify claims]
  F -->|supported| G[Send with citation]
  F -->|unsupported| H[Human handoff]
```

**a) Grounding with RAG and citations.** Fetch the current refund-policy chunk and put it in the prompt. Instruct: "Answer only from the sources below. Quote the section ID for every policy claim." Citations make answers **checkable**, by code and by humans. Grounding cuts hallucination a lot, but not to zero. The model can still misread or overreach the source.

**b) Facts from tools, not memory.** Anything that changes per customer or per day must come from a **tool call** to the real system: order status, delivery date, refund eligibility, price. The model's job is to **choose the tool and phrase the result**, not to know the answer.

**c) "Say I don't know", with examples.** A plain instruction helps. **Examples help more.** Put two or three short demos in the prompt where the right reply is "I don't have that information; let me connect you to an agent." The model copies patterns, so show it the pattern you want.

**d) Constrained outputs.** Ask for structured output, such as JSON with fixed fields: the answer, the cited section IDs, the intent, and a needs-human flag. Then check it in code:

- Every cited section ID must be one that was actually retrieved.
- If a citation is unknown, or there are no citations at all, escalate with "unsupported policy claim".

**Enums** (allowed values like `REFUND`, `RETURN`, `DELIVERY`) stop the model inventing categories. Strict tool schemas plus code checks stop **tool-argument hallucinations**. For example: does this order ID belong to the logged-in user?

**e) Verification step.** Before sending, split the draft into claims. Ask: "is each claim supported by the sources?" This can be a **second model call**, often a smaller, cheaper model used as a judge. It can be simple rules, like "numbers in the answer must appear in the source". Or both. If a claim fails, regenerate once, or fall back to a safe reply.

**f) Confidence thresholds and human handoff.** Combine signals into one decision. Did retrieval find a strong match? Did the verifier pass? Is the intent low-risk? If any signal is weak, **hand off to a human** instead of guessing. For high-risk intents (refunds over a limit, legal or medical topics), hand off by default. A model's own claim ("I'm 90% sure") is not reliable alone. Use **external signals**.

**g) Evals for faithfulness.** Build a test set of real questions with known right answers. Include traps: questions the policy doesn't cover, outdated policies, ambiguous questions. Score each answer for **faithfulness**, **correctness** and **correct abstention**. Run it on every prompt change or model upgrade (see the LLM evals answer).

### Step 4: Measure the hallucination rate

You can't manage what you don't count. A practical definition:

**Hallucination rate = answers with at least one unsupported or false claim / answers checked.**

How to get the number:

- **Offline**: run the eval set (say 500 questions). Score with an LLM judge that has been calibrated against human labels.
- **Online**: sample, say, 1-2% of real chats daily for human review. Oversample risky intents like refunds and cancellations.
- **Proxy signals**: customers saying "that's wrong", repeat contacts on the same issue, agent overrides after handoff, refund disputes.

Track it **per intent**, not just overall. A 1% overall rate can hide 8% on "refund for damaged item".

Also track the **abstention rate**. If you push hallucinations to zero by making the bot refuse everything, you have built an expensive "contact us" page. The goal is a good balance between **wrong answers** and **unnecessary handoffs**.

Every layer adds **latency and cost**. Use the heavy layers where being wrong is expensive (money, legal promises). Use lighter ones for low-risk chat.

## A worked example

**Shreya's support chat on a Flipkart-like marketplace, during a festive sale.** Numbers are illustrative.

Shreya writes: "I bought a phone 10 days ago and the screen has a dead pixel. Can I get a full refund?"

**Version 1, the bad bot.** The prompt only says "You are a helpful support assistant." No documents, no tools. The model replies: "Yes! You can return it within 30 days for a full refund. Your refund will reach you in 3-5 days." Every part is invented. In this example, the real rule is a **7-day replacement-only window for phones**, with a technician visit for display defects. Shreya screenshots the reply. Now the company must honour a policy it never had, or face an angry customer. (This is the animation above.)

**Version 2, the designed bot.** Press Play to follow Shreya's same question through every safeguard:

```anim
{"title": "The designed bot: every claim backed", "w": 680, "h": 400, "intro": "Same question from Shreya. This time facts come from tools and documents, and a verifier checks the draft.",
 "nodes": [
  {"id": "user", "label": "Shreya", "x": 10, "y": 40, "w": 100, "h": 44, "kind": "user"},
```

The same steps in words:

1. **Intent classification**: `RETURN_DEFECT`, category phone. This is marked as a risky intent.
2. **Tool call**: `get_order(user_id)` returns Shreya's recent orders. The bot lists them and asks which one, instead of guessing an order ID. Shreya picks one. `get_return_eligibility(order_id)` returns `{eligible: false, reason: "window_expired", window_days: 7, alternative: "brand_service_center"}`.
3. **Retrieval**: the current phone return-policy chunk, section `RP-PH-3`, plus the warranty section `RP-PH-5`.
4. **Draft**: "Your order is outside the 7-day return window for phones [RP-PH-3], so a refund isn't available. Display defects are covered by the brand warranty; you can visit an authorised service centre [RP-PH-5]."
5. **Verification**: code checks that the cited IDs were actually retrieved, and that "7-day" appears in the source. A small judge model confirms each claim is supported. It passes.
6. **Confidence and handoff**: eligibility came from a tool and the verifier passed. But the topic is a refund, and Shreya is likely upset. So the bot adds: "Would you like me to connect you to an agent to review this?" If yes, the ticket goes over with the order, tool results and draft attached. The human doesn't start from zero.
7. **Measurement**: this chat is in the refund intent, so it is more likely to be sampled for review. Weekly reports show hallucination rate by intent. Once, a new policy was published but not re-indexed, and the "electronics returns" rate jumped. The team then added a **policy freshness check** to the retrieval pipeline.

The key shift: the model went from **being the source of truth** to being **the writer that explains facts produced by systems**.

## Common misconceptions

- **"A bigger or newer model won't hallucinate."** Better models hallucinate less on common facts. None are immune, especially on your private, changing data. System design still matters.
- **"RAG solves hallucination."** It reduces it a lot. The model can still ignore, misread or go beyond the retrieved text. Bad retrieval feeds it the wrong document. You still need citations and verification.
- **"Setting temperature to 0 stops it."** Temperature controls randomness in picking tokens. At 0, the model gives its single most likely answer, which can be wrong every time.
- **"If the model sounds confident, it's probably right."** Fluency and correctness are separate. Use external signals: retrieval match, tool results, the verifier.
- **"Just tell it 'don't hallucinate'."** Instructions help a little. Examples of abstaining, structured outputs and code-side checks help much more.
- **"Zero hallucination is the goal."** Zero is reachable only by refusing to answer. The real goal is a low wrong-answer rate at an acceptable handoff rate, with the strictest controls on high-risk intents.

## How to say it in an interview

*"LLMs are trained to produce likely text, not verified text. When they lack a fact, like a company's refund policy, they produce the most typical-sounding answer with full confidence. Causes include gaps in training data, training that rewards answering over abstaining, long noisy context, and ambiguous questions. So I treat hallucination as a system design problem. In a support bot, policy comes from retrieved documents with required citations. Anything per-customer, like order status or refund eligibility, comes from tool calls, never from the model's memory. I constrain the output to a schema, check in code that citations match what was retrieved, and verify claims on risky intents. If signals are weak, the bot says it isn't sure and hands off to a human with full context. Then I measure hallucination rate per intent, with an offline eval set and daily sampling of real chats. I track it alongside handoff rate, to balance wrong answers against needless escalations."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *How would you detect hallucinations automatically?* Split the answer into claims and check each against the sources with a calibrated judge model. Add rules: every number must appear in the source, and every citation must be one we retrieved. Spot-check the judge with human labels.
- *What if the policy document itself is out of date?* Then the bot is faithfully wrong. Add document owners, effective dates, re-indexing on publish, and alerts when retrieval returns an outdated version.
- *How do you stop the bot promising a refund?* It can't promise one. Only the refund tool can create a refund, and the bot may only report the tool's result. A check blocks any reply with commitment phrases but no matching tool result.

## Key takeaways

- LLMs predict **plausible text, not truth**. A confident tone is not evidence.
- Causes: **training-data gaps, pressure to answer, long context, ambiguous prompts**.
- Types: **factual, unfaithful-to-source, citation, tool-argument, and false "done" claims**.
- **Ground** answers with RAG and **require citations** that code can check.
- **Facts come from tools**: order status, eligibility and prices are never generated.
- Teach **abstention with examples**. **Hand off to humans** on weak signals or risky intents.
- Add **constrained outputs and a verification step** before anything reaches a customer.
- **Measure hallucination rate per intent** alongside handoff rate, offline and in production.

## Check yourself

1. Why does a model state a wrong refund window confidently instead of saying it doesn't know?
   Answer: It is trained to produce likely text, and "You have 30 days to return" is very likely text. It has no built-in truth check, and training often rewards answering over abstaining.
2. The bot has RAG with the correct policy, but still says "full refund" for an item marked "replacement only". What type of hallucination is this, and which layer should catch it?
   Answer: It is unfaithful to the source. A verification step that checks each claim against the retrieved text, plus checked citations, should catch it and block or regenerate the answer.
3. The bot calls get_order with an order ID the customer never mentioned. What prevents this?
   Answer: Strict tool schemas and code-side checks. The order ID must come from the conversation or the user's own order list, and the backend verifies it belongs to the logged-in user.
4. Your hallucination rate dropped to 0.1% after a change, but customer complaints went up. What might have happened?
   Answer: The bot may now refuse or hand off far too often. Check the abstention and handoff rates per intent, because a low hallucination rate means little if the bot stopped answering.

question: How does RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) work?
answer:
## The short answer

Shreya's new TV arrives cracked. She asks the shop's chatbot for a refund. A plain AI model never read this shop's return rules, so it may guess. **RAG fixes that.**

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** works in two moves:

1. **Look up** the few passages from your own documents that match the question.
2. **Paste them into the prompt** and tell the model: answer only from these, and cite them.

The model is a **large language model (LLM)**: software that writes text one small piece at a time. RAG does not change the model. It changes the **evidence the model sees** at the moment of the question.

RAG has two halves:

- **Ingestion (done ahead of time):** clean the documents, cut them into small pieces called **chunks**, turn each chunk into an **embedding** (a list of numbers that captures its meaning), and store them in an **index** with labels such as category and date.
- **Query time (live):** turn the question into numbers too, **fetch the top matching chunks**, **re-sort** them, and let the model **write an answer with citations**.

Why bother? Models have a **knowledge cutoff**, never saw your **private data**, and **hallucinate** (state confident falsehoods) when unsure. Businesses also need **citations**. RAG fixes all four without retraining. The quality of a RAG system is decided mostly by the **retrieval** step, not by the LLM.

## The intuition

Think of an **open-book exam**.

A clever student has read a lot. But they never read your company's policy manual. Ask them about the returns policy and they will bluff.

Now give the same student the right three pages. Say: "Answer from these pages and quote the page number." The answer becomes accurate, and you can check it.

The student is the LLM. **RAG is the librarian** who finds those three pages fast, out of millions.

Words we will use:

- **Token**: a word piece. 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words.
- **Context window**: the most text the model can read in one request. In 2026 it is typically 128K to over 1M tokens. Longer input costs more, and quality can drop.
- **Chunk**: a small piece of a document, often 200-800 tokens, fetched as one unit.
- **Embedding**: a fixed-length list of numbers (say 768 or 1,536) made by an **embedding model**. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers.
- **Vector index**: a store that quickly finds the nearest lists of numbers to the question's list. It usually uses a shortcut method such as **HNSW**, a layered map of neighbours.
- **BM25**: the classic keyword-scoring formula behind search engines such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. It rewards rare words that appear in a document.
- **Reranker**: a slower, more accurate model. It reads the question and each candidate chunk together and scores how relevant the chunk is.
- **Grounding** (or **faithfulness**): every claim in the answer is backed by the fetched text.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why RAG exists

| Problem | What RAG does |
|---|---|
| **Knowledge cutoff** | Fetches today's documents, such as new sale terms, when the question arrives |
| **Private data** never in training | Indexes it in your own store, behind your access rules |
| **Hallucination** | Supplies evidence, and says "if it is not in the sources, say you don't know" |
| **Citations and audit** | Each chunk carries a source ID that the answer cites |

The name comes from a 2020 paper by **Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research**. That paper trained the search part and the writing part together. Today "RAG" usually means something simpler: a ready-made search step feeding a general LLM through the prompt.

### 2. The pipeline in one picture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  D[Policy docs] --> C[Parse and chunk]
  C --> E[Embed chunks]
  E --> I[Hybrid index]
  Q[Shreya question] --> H[Hybrid search top 50]
  I --> H
  H --> K[Rerank to top 5]
  K --> G[LLM answer with citations]
```

### 3. Ingestion: parse, chunk, embed, index

**Parse.** Turn PDFs, web pages, wiki pages, tickets and tables into clean text. Keep the structure: headings, lists, table rows. Bad parsing is a silent killer: a PDF table squashed into word soup is never found.

**Chunk.** Cut the text into pieces that can be fetched. Common choices:

- **Fixed size with overlap**, such as 500 tokens with 50-100 tokens shared between neighbours. Simple and robust.
- **Structure-aware**: cut on headings, sections, FAQ entries or table rows. Then each chunk holds one complete idea.
- **Contextual chunks**: add one line saying where the chunk sits, like "From: Returns Policy > Electronics > Damaged items". Anthropic's **Contextual Retrieval** technique writes this line with an LLM. It reported large drops in failed lookups.

**Embed.** Run each chunk through the embedding model. Use the **same model** for questions and documents. Changing the model means re-embedding everything.

**Index with labels.** Store the numbers, the raw text, and labels called **metadata**: `doc_id`, `section`, `source_url`, `updated_at`, `language`, `category`, plus **access fields** such as `tenant_id` and `allowed_groups`. Metadata lets you filter ("electronics only, current version only") and cite sources.

### 4. Query time: fetch, re-sort, write

Here is the live path for Shreya's question.
